With ofstream's documented default creation mode 0666, the resulting mode is 0666 & ~0022 = 0644 (rw-r--r--), so any non-empty directory/filename/content triple admitted by the line 16 guard produces a secret file readable by all local users, violating the function contract at line 8 ('The file should be accessible only by the current user'). Primary mechanism: CWE-732 incorrect permission assignment.

verdict.summary: On PLATFORM_WEB builds, SetClipboardText builds a JavaScript snippet by interpolating the caller-supplied text into navigator.clipboard.writeText('%s') with no escaping and passes it to emscripten_run_script, which executes it as script. Any text containing a single quote (and following script) is executed as JavaScript in the page, e.g. text = "'); alert(1); //" produces navigator.clipboard.writeText(''); alert(1); //').

evidence.reason: The parameter text (line 1, const char*, residual range = any C string; the shown code imposes no NULL, length, or content check) is substituted verbatim by the printf-family TextFormat into the literal format string "navigator.clipboard.writeText('%s')" — preserving every byte, including the unescaped single quote that closes the JS string literal — and the resulting string is executed by emscripten_run_script. Witness: text = "'); alert(1); //" becomes navigator.clipboard.writeText(''); alert(1); //'), executing alert(1) in the page. No guard exists between input and sink, so the witness passes every (absent) check; the single-quote delimiter survives unneutralized, confirming CWE-94 code injection at this sink statement.

assumptions: The PLATFORM_WEB preprocessor branch (line 6) selects the emscripten path for web builds; the analysis of line 7 applies only to that build configuration.
TextFormat is used as a printf-family formatter (per its name and the %s argument at line 7): it substitutes %s with the string content of text and performs no escaping or truncation.
text is a NUL-terminated C string, consistent with its %s usage at line 7.
limitations: Whether an actual attacker controls text is caller-dependent: the fragment shows no entry point, so the confirmed injection is established by residual-range analysis of the unconstrained internal-helper parameter, not by a demonstrated attacker input path.

A NULL text value passed to %s is not a confirmed NULL dereference: nothing in the shown code produces NULL; only an out-of-scope caller could supply it, and the fragment neither checks nor dereferences it.
Any internal-buffer overflow inside TextFormat is unconfirmable: the callee body and its capacities are not shown in the fragment.
The desktop path (line 4, glfwSetClipboardString) has no injection or memory-safety sink visible in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled 32-bit header fields wrap before width conversion: with frames=0x40000001, the frames*4 allocation (line 29) wraps to 4 bytes while the loop (lines 33-34) writes ~4 GiB of 32-bit file values past it, a heap buffer overflow at line 34 (CWE-787, integer wrap CWE-190); independently, treesize in [0xFFFFFFF0, 0xFFFFFFFF] wraps treesize+16 (line 76) into a deca byte allocation and a negative length, so get_buffer writes file bytes past the block (CWE-787); the frames>0xFFFFFF check at line 16 only logs (no return shown), so no shown statement bounds either value.

assumptions: fields assigned from get_le32(pb) are 32-bit wide (evidenced by the (int32_t) cast at line 14; the (int32_t)get_le32(pb) value domain is 0..0xFFFFFFFF), so frames*4 (line 29) and treesize+16 (line 70) are computed in 32-bit arithmetic and wrap; the fragment shows no return.

st->index (line 40) after the body-less if(!st) (line 39), ast[i]->index/frame (lines 59-60) after un-tested av_new_stream, and frm_flags writes (lines 30, line 36) if av_malloc fails: NULL dereferences dependent on allocator failure states produced by attacker-sized allocations — noted, not added to cwe[].

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability is confirmable within the fragment. User input `subdomain_prefix` is gated by `std::regex_match` against the literal class `[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+ (L19/L22), which excludes every URL-authority metacharacter ("@", "/", ":", "?", "#", CR/LF, whitespace), so the generated host is always the trusted `domain` or a subdomain suffix of it, and only bytes in [a-zA-Z0-9.-] can reach the stdout sink (L44); no redirect, server-side request, or log sink exists in the fragment, and there are no memory-safety, crypto, or loop sinks. The regex at L19 (`^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+$`) is used with `std::regex_match` (full-string match, L22), so it admits exactly non-empty strings over {a-zA-Z0-9, '.', '-'}.
limitations: CWE-601/918/117 via the generated URL cannot be confirmed: the fragment never consumes the URL in a redirect (Location header), a server-side HTTP request, or a log write; only `std::cout << url` (L44) is present, and any dangerous downstream consumer is outside the fragment.

Line 26 (memmove) operates on maddr->user whose capacity is not declared in the fragment, but the copy lies within the existing string extent, so no overflow is derivable either way.

The source-route collapse at lines 23-27 and the 'no domain, local user' acceptance at lines 39-44 can re-normalize attacker-chosen text (e.g., '<:victim@dom>' becomes 'victim@dom'); whether this is a validation bypass depends on the unshown valid_localpart/valid_domainpart semantics and downstream routing, so no CWE is assignable.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table uses ref_count[list] as the loop bound (line 27) with no upper cap in the shown code, so i can reach values where the frame-expansion index 16 + 2*i (lines 71-72, 75) overflows signed int and wraps to a negative subscript, which is then used as the first index in array stores into pwt->luma_weight/pwt->chroma_weight, causing an out-of-bounds write (memory corruption). Primary CWE-190: integer overflow corrupting a security-relevant index consumed by an array-subscript sink.

evidence.reason: Sink: array store whose first subscript is derived from the loop counter i (int), which is bounded only by line 27's `i < ref_count[list]` with ref_count[list] retaining the full int domain (Phase 1, no cap in the fragment). At i = 1073741824 (reached when ref_count[0] = 1073741825, admitted by line 27, with luma_weight_flag=0, chroma_format_idc=0, picture_structure=PICT_FRAME so lines 30/45/70 admit), 2*i = 2147483648 wraps to -2147483648 and 16 + 2*i evaluates to -2147483632, an out-of-domain negative index used in a store — signed-overflow-to-corrupted-index (CWE-190) producing an out-of-bounds write; capacity of luma_weight is not declared in the fragment, so the exact excess is unquantifiable but the negative index is provably invalid.

Same confirmed mechanism as line 71: for i = 1073741824 the index expression 16 + 2*i and 16 + 2*i + 1 wrap in int arithmetic (2*i overflows INT_MAX) to -2147483632 and -2147483631, which are consumed as the first subscript of luma_weight in a store (CWE-190; OOB write; exact excess not quantifiable because the member declaration is outside the fragment).

Same confirmed CWE-190 mechanism on the chroma array when sps->chroma_format_idc is nonzero (admitted at line 73): at i = 1073741824 the index 16 + 2*i overflows signed int to -2147483632 and is used as the first subscript in a store, causing an out-of-bounds write before chroma_weight; the array capacity is not declared in the fragment, so only the negative-index corruption is confirmable.

assumptions: 32-bit two's-complement int arithmetic: ISO C makes signed overflow UB, but the wrap used for the witness is the standard implementation outcome; confidence is capped accordingly.
ref_count points to an array with valid ref_count[0] and ref_count[1] reads (caller contract; not shown in the fragment).
get_ue_golomb/get_bits1/get_se_golomb follow their standard FFmpeg semantics (unsigned/int returns; return values are consumed immediately in the shown assignments).
picture_structure = PICT_FRAME is a valid int-compatible program constant used by the guard at line 70; its numeric value is not needed for the equality to hold.
sps is treated as non-NULL since the fragment contains no NULL producer for it.
limitations: The direct out-of-bounds write/read of luma_weight/chroma_weight for moderate ref_count values (e.g., exceeding the real array size) cannot be confirmed because the declarations/capacities of pwt->luma_weight and pwt->chroma_weight are not present in the fragment (no CWE attached).
The OOB read of pwt->luma_weight[i][list][0] on the RHS of line 71 at large i is likewise unconfirmable without the member capacity.

verdict.summary: In SKIP_TYPE_ROW/SKIP_TYPE_COL, the per-row/column guard only verifies 1 remaining bit before reading the skip flag, but the else branch then reads mb_width/mb_height additional bits via get_bits1 with no availability check, so an admitted short bitstream drives the bit reader past the available data (out-of-bounds bitstream read).

The only guard on this path, line 24 (`if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;`), admits bits_left >= 1 and covers only the flag read at line 26; the else branch (mb_width iterations of line 33) consumes 1 + mb_width bits in total. Capacity reference: the available-data bound is the count returned by get_bits_left, which the line-24 guard proves to be only >= 1.

Same mechanism as the ROW case, transposed: line 39 (`if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;`) admits bits_left >= 1 and covers only the column flag read at line 41, while the else branch reads mb_height bits via line 48 without per-iteration verification. verdict.summary: Log injection (CWE-117): the RADIUS User-Name value is copied verbatim into `name` at line 27 and passed unmodified as a `%s` argument to `radlog`/`radlog_request` on the reject paths (lines 39, 76-77, 95-96, 108, 119). Newline/CR bytes in the user name are never escaped or truncated, so an attacker can forge or poison RADIUS log entries.

evidence.snippet:
radlog_request(L_AUTH, 0, request, "[%s]: invalid shell [%s]",
		       name, pwd->pw_shell);
evidence.reason: CWE-117 primary sink. `name` (char * from `request->username->vp_strvalue`, line 27) is a NUL-terminated byte string whose content is unconstrained by any shown check (only the non-NULL username guard at line 23 applies). The witness `name = "attacker\r\nFORGED-LOG"` passes every guard on the path (line 23 non-NULL, line 43 `getpwnam` non-NULL, lines 59-60 shadow lookup non-returning, lines 87-94 loop exits with `shell == NULL` which line 94 admits), and reaches this `%s` argument with its CR/LF bytes intact because the only transformation in the shown code is the bare assignment at line 27. The printf-family callee prints all bytes up to the NUL verbatim, enabling forged log entries / monitoring evasion.

Same CWE-117 mechanism at the DENY_SHELL reject path: `name` (line 27, unconstrained User-Name bytes) is passed unmodified as `%s`. The guard at line 75 admits `pw_shell == DENY_SHELL`, which is a library/config-supplied value; once admitted, the sink logs `name` verbatim, preserving newline/CR control bytes for log forgery.

evidence.snippet: radlog_request(L_AUTH, 0, request, "[%s]: password has expired", name);
evidence.reason: Same CWE-117 mechanism on the shadow-expiry reject path (admitted when `spwd->sp_expire > 0` and `request->timestamp / 86400 > spwd->sp_expire`, lines 106-107): `name` (line 27, unconstrained User-Name bytes) reaches the `%s` sink with no escaping, preserving CR/LF bytes for log injection.

evidence.snippet: radlog_request(L_AUTH, 0, request, "[%s]: password has expired", name);
evidence.reason: Same CWE-117 mechanism on the FreeBSD/bsdi/_PWF_EXPIRE expiry reject path (admitted when `pwd->pw_expire > 0` and `request->timestamp > pwd->pw_expire`, lines 117-118): `name` (line 27, unconstrained User-Name bytes) reaches the `%s` sink unmodified, so CR/LF control bytes survive to the log output.

Same CWE-117 mechanism on the OSFC2 account-lock path (admitted by `pr_pw->uflg.fg_lock != 1`, line 38): `name` (line 27, unconstrained User-Name bytes) is passed unmodified as `%s`, so CR/LF bytes in the user name are written verbatim into the log, enabling log-line forgery.

assumptions: `request->username->vp_strvalue` is a NUL-terminated C string; the fragment's own usage as a C string (line 27, `strlen` at line 59, indexing at line 129) implies the string-termination invariant.

Library/OS-returned struct fields (`pw_passwd`, `sp_pwdp`, `pw_shell`, `fd_encrypt`, `pw_expire`) are treated as non-NULL per the analysis rules; the fragment shows no statement establishing a NULL minimum, and no statement marks them nullable.

`radlog`/`radlog_request` are printf-family log writers whose callee behavior is not shown; the finding anchors at the call sites where the shown code derives and forwards `name` unmodified as a `%s` argument.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The fragment performs per-event bounds validation (line 53: dataLeft must be >= size*2 before the 4- or 8-byte swaps at lines 56-57/60-61), the dataLeft arithmetic is mod-4 invariant so the size==1 guard/consume mismatch cannot underflow or bypass the guard, the request minimum length is enforced at line 6, and the only log sink uses a fixed format literal. The exact numeric values of XkbMapNotifyMask/XkbMapNotify/enum cases are not shown; the analysis only relies on their mutual consistency (the bit removed at line 24 matches the event skipped at line 26), which holds for any consistent definitions.
Unchecked/unobservable framework invariants (macro bodies, dispatcher buffer sizing) are the only external premises; no claim in the safe verdict depends on a more restrictive caller contract.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability can be confirmed from the fragment. The six writes to mb_type[mb_y * s->mb_stride + mb_x] (L11-12, L17-18, L24-25, L28-29, L37-38, L41-42) are indexed by internal decoder fields s->mb_height/mb_width/mb_stride that the fragment neither constrains nor bounds, and the capacity of mb_type is never shown (only its pointer initialization at L5). assumptions: get_bits(&s->gb, 2) returns a value in {0,1,2,3} per the 2-bit read argument (L6), so the switch at L7 covers the full admitted set.
get_bits1(&s->gb) returns a value in {0,1} (L18, L22, L29, L35, L41).

Bitstream over-read through get_bits/get_bits1 cannot be analyzed: the callee bodies and the bit-buffer size are not in the fragment.
Resource-exhaustion (huge loop bounds) would require attacker-controlled or demonstrably unbounded dimensions, which the fragment does not establish.
NULL dereference of s->current_picture_ptr (L5) has no NULL-producing path inside the shown code and is out of scope.

verdict.summary: The only injection sink is emscripten_run_script on line 9, which evaluates a script built from user text inside a single-quoted JS string literal. The line-8 guard excludes any text containing byte 0x27, the only character that can terminate that literal, so no witness passes the guard and executes injected code; a trailing backslash produces only a SyntaxError and escape sequences decode inside the literal value. No confirmed vulnerability is derivable from the shown fragment.

assumptions: emscripten_run_script evaluates its argument as JavaScript (eval context) per its documented contract, and attacker-controlled bytes reach the evaluated script only inside the single-quoted literal delimited by the TextFormat format string on line 9.
text is a NUL-terminated C string per the function signature (line 1); the shown code reads it via strchr on line 8 and as the %s argument on line 9.
limitations: JS-injection candidate (CWE-94/CWE-79) demoted: no concrete witness passes the line-8 guard and still executes injected statements. The guard's excluded set (any string containing byte 0x27) equals the set required to terminate a single-quoted JS string; '\u0027'-style escapes decode to a quote inside the literal without ending it, and text ending in '\' escapes the generated closing quote, yielding an unterminated literal (SyntaxError, no code execution).
A very long text could overflow TextFormat's internal destination buffer, but that buffer's capacity is not declared in the fragment, so no byte-level overflow claim can be confirmed.
NULL text is not producible anywhere within the shown code and is therefore not analyzed as a finding.
Rejecting legitimate clipboard text containing apostrophes (e.g. "don't") is a functional limitation of the filter, not a security vulnerability.
The analysis assumes a pure JS-eval context for emscripten_run_script; a different embedding (e.g., HTML script-tag insertion) is not indicated by the shown code.

The only fully evaluable input-derived computation, `stuff->numSpecs * sizeof(ctx.specs[0])` at line 12, is protected by the overflow guard at line 9 whose admitted set (numSpecs <= UINT32_MAX / sizeof(spec)) keeps the product within UINT32_MAX. No loop structures are present in the fragment, so loop-termination analysis is vacuous.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable in the fragment. The only security-relevant operation is the fixed 1-byte read of p[1] at line 8, reached whenever MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) == 2; however, the fragment contains no capacity declaration or bound for the object p points to, so an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) cannot be established — the boundary claim is unconfirmable rather than demonstrated. Any caller contract guaranteeing at least two valid bytes at p (e.g., a well-formed NUL-terminated string in which a lead byte is always followed by a second byte or the terminator) is outside the fragment and was not used in either verdict direction.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown fragment. verdict.summary: ff_er_add_slice at line 100 receives slice-end coordinates derived from s->mb_x-1 and s->mb_y with no shown guard on the wrap case: mb_count==0 with mb_x==0, or a full run to the picture end (mb_count==left), leaves mb_x==0 (end_x == -1) and can leave mb_y==mb_height. These values are outside the valid MB-index domains [0, mb_width-1] and [0, mb_height-1] for the per-MB error tables the callee indexes, producing an out-of-bounds access (CWE-787) whose in-fragment derivation is exact.

evidence.snippet: ff_er_add_slice(s, start_mb_x, s->resync_mb_y, s->mb_x-1, s->mb_y, AC_END|DC_END|MV_END);
evidence.reason: s->mb_x-1 and s->mb_y reach this sink with out-of-domain values for MB-grid indices. mb_count is admitted as 0 by the guards at lines 11 (mb_count < 0 rejected) and 22 (mb_count > left rejected; left = mb_width*mb_height - mb_pos at line 21); with mb_width=1, mb_height=1, mb_x=0, mb_y=0, the position guard at lines 15-16 admits mb_x=0 (0 < 1), the loop at line 70 is skipped, and s->mb_x-1 evaluates to -1. Alternatively with mb_count == left, after decoding the final MB the wrap at lines 91-95 leaves mb_x=0 and mb_y==mb_height, so the sink receives end_x=-1 and end_y=mb_height. The grid capacity used by the callee is mb_width x mb_height (per the arithmetic at lines 20-21); -1 and mb_height are outside [0, mb_width-1] and [0, mb_height-1], so the argument derivation is out of the domain required of an index parameter, making this an out-of-bounds read-modify-write in per-MB error-state storage (CWE-787).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown fragment. No input-derived index, size, length, format string, path, URL, or discarded return status exists in the fragment.

assumptions: SSH_PACKET_CALLBACK supplies session and packet as framework-provided arguments; per the framework-pointer rule, session and its fields (including next_crypto) are treated as non-NULL because no statement in the fragment marks them nullable.
The line 7 guard constrains session->dh_handshake_state to exactly {DH_STATE_INIT} for the code after the guard; all other values are diverted to the error label at line 9.
The switch at line 11 constrains session->next_crypto->kex_type to the enumerated cases (lines 12-25); every other value is handled by the fail-closed default at lines 26-28.
SSH_ERROR (lines 2, 28) is the failure sentinel compared at line 32, and SSH_PACKET_USED (line 36) is the packet-consumption return per the callback macro contract visible in the fragment.
limitations: NULL dereference of session->next_crypto at line 11 is unconfirmable: no statement in the fragment allocates, frees, assigns, or NULL-checks next_crypto, so no NULL-producer path exists inside the shown code (CWE-476 would require one).

Memory-safety or injection flaws arising from parsing of the attacker-controlled packet (e.g., the client DH public value) would materialize inside ssh_server_kexdh_init / ssh_server_ecdh_init / ssh_server_curve25519_init (lines 14/18/23), whose bodies are not shown; the fragment derives no index/size/length from the packet, so no out-of-domain call-site argument is confirmable.

A kex type not covered by the switch cases (e.g., newer DH-group algorithms in later libssh versions) reaches the default case and terminates the connection; this is a versioning/availability concern, not a confirmed security flaw, and kex_type is internally negotiated state.

The consistency of dh_handshake_state with the negotiated kex_type (e.g., that next_crypto exists while dh_handshake_state == DH_STATE_INIT) is established outside the fragment and is not verifiable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability is demonstrable inside this fragment. The candidates that could matter - integer wrap of the lnum arithmetic, u_save receiving boundary values (0 / ml_line_count+1), and the discarded format_lines status - depend on callee bodies or type widths not shown in the fragment, so they are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: The fragment declares only `oparg_T *oap`, `int keep_cursor`, and `long old_line_count`; oparg_T, linenr_T, pos_T, and win_T are used but their definitions, including the width of linenr_T, are not shown, and no capacity or type-width invariant was imported from outside the fragment.

The bodies of u_save, format_lines, redraw_curbuf_later, beginline, msgmore, check_cursor, and the FOR_ALL_WINDOWS macro are outside the fragment; call-site analysis is limited to the arguments the fragment derives.
limitations: Integer wrap of `(oap->start.lnum - 1)` (line 11) or `(oap->end.lnum + 1)` (line 12) is unconfirmable: the width of linenr_T and any maximum constant are not declared in the fragment, and a wrapped value would be consumed only inside u_save (body not shown), so no security-relevant consumption is demonstrable.

When `oap->start.lnum == 1`, line 11 passes top == 0 to u_save, and when `oap->end.lnum` equals the current line count, line 12 passes bot == ml_line_count + 1; whether the callee accepts these boundary values is not visible in the fragment, so neither a finding nor a protective claim can be anchored.

`beginline`/`check_cursor` (lines 36/50) and the cursor restores (line 46) may operate on input-derived cursor line numbers, but the fragment shows no buffer/line-array capacity and no guard validating the cursor line against a capacity, so no OOB claim is groundable.
No format-string, command/argument, SQL/NoSQL/XPath, SSRF, path/file, crypto, or authn/authz sink exists in the fragment, so those classes are out of scope by absence.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the audio-stream loop dereferences the unchecked av_new_stream() result at line 70, and the frm_size/frm_flags buffers allocated at lines 36-37 are written without NULL checks at lines 41 and 44. For attacker-controlled rates[]/frames fields that pass the guards at lines 68 and 32, an allocation failure crashes the demuxer, enabling a denial of service on crafted SMK input.

evidence.reason: rates[i] is entry-point input via get_le32 (line 29, full uint32 domain). The guard at line 68 admits e.g. rates[0]=1, so av_new_stream(s,0) is called at line 69; the fragment itself proves that call is nullable via the if(!st) check at line 48, but here the result is dereferenced at line 70 with no NULL check, producing a NULL-pointer dereference on allocation failure (CWE-476).

frames is entry-point input (line 14) and line 32 admits every value <= 0xFFFFFF, e.g. frames=1. av_malloc(smk->frames*4) at line 36 is never NULL-checked, so when the allocation fails the loop at lines 40-42 writes through the NULL frm_size pointer at line 41 (CWE-476).

Same unchecked-allocation pattern: av_malloc(smk->frames) at line 37 is not NULL-checked; for an admitted frames value (e.g. 1) the loop at lines 43-45 writes through the possibly-NULL frm_flags pointer at line 44 (CWE-476).

assumptions: SmackerContext field types (frames, treesize, rates, ...) are not declared in the fragment; get_le32 returns uint32, so fields are treated as 32-bit values.

The caps at line 20 (treesize < UINT_MAX/4) and line 32 (frames <= 0xFFFFFF) are the only bounds the fragment imposes; the byte-level accounting shows exact-fit writes for all admitted values when allocations succeed.
av_new_stream() is nullable per line 48 and av_malloc() per line 85; no non-NULL invariant is established for the call at line 69 or the allocations at lines 36-37.
limitations: The NULL-deref witnesses require the allocation (av_new_stream/av_malloc) to fail, an environment-dependent condition the fragment cannot force; confidence is capped accordingly.

If 'frames' were a signed 32-bit int, negative values would pass the line 32 check; the frame loops would not execute and frm_size/frm_flags would remain NULL for later (unshown) use - unconfirmable here.

The extradata allocation admits up to ~1 GiB (line 20 permits treesize up to UINT_MAX/4-1 and line 83 adds 16); bounded, single-shot, and environment-dependent, so it is recorded as a robustness concern, not CWE-400.
The short-read error path at lines 92-95 frees frm_size/frm_flags but not st->codec->extradata - a single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled volume in the shown code.
smk->pts_inc = -smk->pts_inc (line 59) wraps for INT32_MIN, but the corrupted value only feeds av_reduce/av_set_pts_info (timing metadata), not a security sink.
SMK_AUD_BINKAUD/PACKED/STEREO/16BITS bit positions are not defined in the fragment; the guard at line 68 has a non-empty admitted set regardless of their values.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment alone. The only notable pattern is freeing `name` (line 11) after handing a struct whose `.name` points to it into `type_register(&ti)` (lines 5, 10); whether that is a use-after-free depends entirely on the unshown contract of `type_register` (retains vs. copies `ti.name`), so it cannot be anchored to a shown sink and is recorded in limitations. Null/missing `m->name`, OOM in `g_strconcat`, and the discarded `type_register` return value are likewise unconfirmable as findings within the fragment.

assumptions: `g_strconcat` (line 3) returns a NUL-terminated heap allocation of exactly `strlen(m->name) + strlen(TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX) + 1` bytes when it succeeds (glib contract in the visible use), and `g_free(name)` (line 11) is the matching, single free.
`TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX`, `TYPE_MACHINE`, and `machine_class_init` (lines 3, 6, 7) are valid, type-compatible constants/pointers; their definitions are not shown.
`m` is an internal-helper parameter; the fragment neither dereferences `m` beyond `m->name` (line 3) nor constrains it.
limitations: Use-after-free (CWE-416) of `name` after `g_free(name)` (line 11) is unconfirmable: it requires `type_register` (line 10) to retain `ti.name` (or the stack-local `ti` itself) beyond the call and dereference it later, and no statement in the fragment shows retention, copying, or any use of `name`/`ti` after line 11 — the lifetime contract of the callee is not visible.

NULL dereference of `m`/`m->name` inside `g_strconcat` (line 3) is unconfirmable: no shown code path produces a NULL `m->name`; a NULL could only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller, so it is a defensive-hardening/caller-precondition concern.

A NULL result from `g_strconcat` under allocation failure (line 3) would make `ti.name` NULL at line 5; `type_register`'s behavior on a NULL name is not shown, and this requires an unchecked allocation to fail, which is out of scope.

The return value of `type_register(&ti)` (line 10) is discarded and success is returned unconditionally (line 12), but the callee's failure semantics are not shown and no security-relevant operation is shown to run on a failure state, so no error/status-handling flaw is confirmable.

verdict.summary: The header validation checks at lines 11-13, 14-17 and 20-22 only call av_log and never return in this fragment, so attacker-controlled mb_count / s->mb_x / s->mb_y retain their full int domains. Downstream, the slice-registration call at line 92 consumes end coordinates derived entirely in the shown code: s->mb_x-1 evaluates to -1 when mb_count <= 0 (loop at line 63 skipped), and s->mb_y equals mb_height when mb_count == mb_width*mb_height + 1 (loop increments y past the grid since the COUNT ERROR guard does not stop execution). Both values are out of the MB-grid coordinate domain this fragment itself states at line 15, yet reach ff_er_add_slice, whose coordinates are consumed as indices into the slice-error tables - an OOB memory access (CWE-787). The same out-of-grid position drives ff_update_block_index/MPV_decode_mb inside the last loop iteration.

evidence.snippet: ff_er_add_slice(s, start_mb_x, s->resync_mb_y, s->mb_x-1, s->mb_y, AC_END|DC_END|MV_END);
evidence.reason: s->mb_x and s->mb_y originate from the header decoders (lines 8/10) driven by the attacker buffer and are never constrained: lines 11-13, 14-17 and 20-22 only log and no return exists before this call. Witness A: mb_count=0, mb_x=0, mb_y=0 passes every guard and skips the loop (line 63), so line 92 computes end_x = s->mb_x - 1 = -1 (exact int arithmetic). Witness B: mb_count = mb_width*mb_height + 1 with mb_x=mb_y=0 passes guard 11 and 14-15; guard 20 (mb_count > left) also fires but only logs, and the loop (63-91) advances the position once per iteration via the wrap at 83-85, ending with s->mb_y == mb_height before line 92 passes end_y = mb_height - the value line 15 flags as invalid (s->mb_y >= s->mb_height). ff_er_add_slice consumes these parameters as slice start/end coordinates/indexes into the per-MB error tables, so -1 and mb_height are out of the domain the operation requires; the fragment gives no later protective check (90 breaks only on SLICE_END). This is a confirmed out-of-domain index derivation at the call site => OOB access, CWE-787 primary; the exact byte/entry excess is unquantifiable because the error table capacity is not declared in the fragment.

Same taint and missing-return root cause as the line 92 sink. Under Witness B (mb_count = mb_width*mb_height + 1, mb_x=mb_y=0, guards 11/14-15 pass, 20 logs only), the position wrap at lines 83-85 places (mb_x, mb_y) = (0, mb_height) at iteration mb_width*mb_height+1, so this statement runs with a y-coordinate exactly one row beyond the grid admitted by line 15 (valid y in [0, mb_height-1]). MPV_decode_mb consumes the MB coordinates as the destination for writing the decoded macroblock into the frame buffer; out-of-grid coordinates mean the resulting frame-buffer write is out of bounds (CWE-787). It also executes even when ret == SLICE_ERROR (lines 75-77 log only), compounding the failed-state decode.

assumptions: rv10_decode_picture_header / rv20_decode_picture_header return an int MB count and can output mb_count=0 or mb_count=mb_width*mb_height+1 with mb_x=mb_y=0 for attacker-chosen bitstreams; nothing in the fragment excludes any int value (lines 11-13 and 20-22 are log-only).
The primary witnesses take mb_width, mb_height >= 1 (int values in the header-decoder output domain, not excluded by any shown statement).

ff_er_add_slice / ff_update_block_index / MPV_decode_mb treat their x/y arguments as macroblock-grid indices/coordinates per their names and the call-site usage; their bodies are not part of the fragment.
s = avctx->priv_data is non-NULL per codec-framework contract; current_picture_ptr is explicitly NULL-checked at line 24 before dereference.
A bitstream that keeps ret != SLICE_END (including SLICE_ERROR, which is only logged at lines 75-77) is attacker-selectable, so loop-exit at line 90 does not fire for the witnesses.
limitations: The allocation capacity of ff_er_add_slice's error-status table and of the frame buffers is not declared in this fragment, so the exact overflow extent (index == capacity + N) cannot be quantified; the confirmed part is the out-of-domain coordinate/index derivation at the call sites, per call-site confirmation.

buf_size*8 (line 6) and 8*buf_size2 (lines 70-72) overflow int for |buf_size| >= 2^28, but the corrupted negative value only flows into s->gb.size_in_bits comparisons and the return value; no in-fragment memory operation consumes it directly, and downstream get_bits behavior is unshown (CWE-190 candidate not confirmed).

Line 29-30 (if(MPV_frame_start(s, avctx) < 0) ff_er_frame_start(s);) continues into decoding on a failed frame start instead of returning; any NULL dereference or corrupted-state dereference would occur inside unshown callees (CWE-754-style error handling, unconfirmed).
MPV_decode_mb after SLICE_ERROR with in-grid coordinates is a decode-of-garbage robustness issue, not a memory-safety issue by itself; its out-of-grid variant is covered by the primary finding.
mb_count up to INT_MAX makes the loop run very long (CPU-exhaustion potential), but the loop is finite (counts down), so no CWE-835; the practical magnitude depends on the unshown header decoders.
Zero or negative mb_width/mb_height header outcomes would also defeat the index discipline, but grid capacities and header internals are not visible, so those variants are not asserted.
Reading with buf_size <= 0 (negative bit size into init_get_bits) is outside what the fragment itself can be shown to guard.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in rpmPackageFilesInstall: the file index fx returned by rpmfiNext() is bounded only by the loop guards (fx >= 0, lines 23/65/155/169/190), while fdata is allocated with exactly fc elements (xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata)), line 15). Any iterator index fx >= fc — e.g. fc=1, fx=1, admitted by the guard — reaches &fdata[fx] (lines 24/66/156/170/191) and the subsequent fp->... writes land past the heap object, giving memory corruption from a crafted package (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Primary sink. fx = rpmfiNext(fi) (line 65) has residual range [0, INT_MAX] because the only visible constraint is the guard 'fx >= 0'; fdata's capacity is fc elements from 'xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata))' at line 15 (valid indices 0..fc-1). Witness fc=1, fx=1 passes the guard and indexes element 1 of a 1-element array; writes through fp (e.g. fp->stage = FILE_UNPACK at line 146) then write past the heap object by at least sizeof(struct filedata_s) bytes. CWE-787 out-of-bounds write: the subscript argument is not provably in-domain for the admitted set [0, INT_MAX].

Same OOB-write pattern in the collection loop: fx from rpmfiNext (line 23) is only lower-bounded by '>= 0'; capacity is fc elements (line 15). An admitted value fx >= fc writes through fp (fp->action, fp->fpath, fp->stage at lines 26/28/29/33/44) past the allocation. CWE-787.

Same OOB-write pattern in the setmeta loop: fx from rpmfiNext (line 155) is bounded only by '>= 0' against a fc-element fdata (line 15); fp->stage = FILE_PREP (line 163) writes out of bounds for any admitted fx >= fc. CWE-787.

Same OOB-write pattern in the commit loop: fx from rpmfiNext (line 169) is only lower-bounded by '>= 0'; capacity is fc elements (line 15); fp->stage = FILE_COMMIT (line 181) writes out of bounds for admitted fx >= fc. CWE-787.

Same OOB-write pattern in the backward cleanup walk: fx from rpmfiNext (line 190) is bounded only by '>= 0'; capacity is fc elements (line 15). Reads/writes through fp (line 193, 199) for admitted fx >= fc are out of bounds. CWE-787.

assumptions: fdata's capacity is fc elements, from 'struct filedata_s *fdata = xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata));' at line 15; valid indices are 0..fc-1.
xcalloc zero-initializes fdata, so fields such as fp->stage, fp->skip and fp->suffix are defined before first use.
RPMERR_ITER_END is a negative sentinel, so the '>= 0' loop guards terminate iteration on end-of-iteration.
fc = rpmfilesFC(files) (line 10) derives from the same 'files' object, but no shown statement ties rpmfiNext(fi)'s maximum index to fc.
limitations: The positive verdict rests on the Phase-1 residual-range rule: rpmfiNext's index keeps its full declared int domain minus the visible '>= 0' guard ([0, INT_MAX]). Whether the unshown rpmfi/rpmfiles implementation can actually return fx >= fc is a library contract not visible here; if that contract guarantees 0..fc-1, the flaw is unreachable. This caps confidence at 0.6.
NULL dereference of *failedFile at lines 143/162/183: a NULL failedFile can only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller; not a fragment-confirmed producer.

fi = rpmfilesIter(...) at line 22 is used by rpmfiNext at line 23 without the NULL check that later guards lines 54-58; a crash would require the unshown call to fail for some input, which the fragment does not demonstrate.

Masked return status: rc from rpmfiStat (line 36) is overwritten by rpmpluginsCallFsmFilePre (line 42); on stat failure with a successful plugin call, processing continues with a zeroed sb, but the only downstream effects shown are the UNKNOWN_FILETYPE error path (line 128) or FA_TOUCH metadata handling — no confirmed security-relevant operation runs on the failure state.

Log-injection concern at lines 87-88: the rpmlog format string is constant and fp->fpath is a %s argument; newline/control characters in package file names and the log sink's behavior are not established in the fragment.
Negative fc into xcalloc(fc, ...) (line 15): xcalloc failure/abort semantics and rpmfilesFC failure behavior are unshown; no security-relevant operation is shown running on that failure state.

Path-handling and filesystem sinks (fsmMkdir, fsmSymlink, fsmMknod, fsmCommit, fsmRemove, etc.) receive package-derived paths, but their callee internals (path traversal, symlink following) are outside the fragment and unconfirmed.
fp->fpath leak/overwrite on duplicate iterator indices depends on unshown iterator behavior and is bounded without volume amplification.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown fragment. qemu_register_machine() concatenates m->name with the constant TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX into TypeInfo.name via g_strconcat (line 4) and registers it (line 9); the fragment performs no arithmetic, has no branches or loops, and contains no injection, format-string, crypto, or path/command sinks. Concerns about NULL m/m->name, the unconditional return 0, the un-freed name string, and a possible duplicate-type abort in type_register are all caller- or callee-dependent and are not producible or confirmable within the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: g_strconcat (line 4) returns a freshly allocated NUL-terminated heap string sized exactly to the concatenation of its non-NULL arguments, per its standard library contract.

TypeInfo (lines 3-8) is an aggregate whose fields name, parent, class_init, and class_data are consumed as initialized; TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX and TYPE_MACHINE are compile-time constants not shown in the fragment.
qemu_register_machine is called once per machine definition; the fragment shows no caller that supplies attacker-controlled QEMUMachine values.
limitations: NULL m or NULL m->name: the fragment imposes no check on either, but no producer of NULL exists within the shown code; both are only caller-suppliable, which is out of scope, and g_strconcat's standard contract terminates on a NULL argument rather than dereferencing it.

Any crash or abort inside type_register (line 9), including from an empty or duplicate type name, depends on unshown callee behavior and on values (duplicate names, NULL names) whose provenance is not established in the fragment; not confirmable.

The heap string returned by g_strconcat (line 4) is never freed in the shown code; if type_register does not take ownership this is a memory leak, but it is a one-time-per-registration leak that does not compound with attacker-controlled volume, so it is not a finding.

Unconditional `return 0` (line 10): type_register's return type and failure modes are unshown, and no step in the fragment can fail while still reaching line 10, so no error/status-handling flaw can be demonstrated.
No capacity, bound, or minimum-length invariant for m->name is visible in the fragment, so no overflow, truncation, or off-by-one claim could be capacity-grounded either way.

verdict.summary: The file index fx yielded by rpmfiNext is constrained only by '>= 0' (line 24) and is never bounded against the fdata allocation count fc (line 10/15); &fdata[fx] at lines 25, 68, 170, 184 and 205 is consequently reachable with fx >= fc (e.g., fc == 1, fx == 1), writing struct fields one or more elements past the allocated heap array during package install — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787): fdata has exactly fc elements allocated at line 15 (xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata))). fx is the return of rpmfiNext (line 24) with residual range [0, INT_MAX] after the >= 0 guard; no shown statement bounds fx above, so fx == fc is admitted and indexes one past capacity, and subsequent stores through fp (e.g., fp->action at 27/29) write past the allocation.

Same heap OOB write (CWE-787) as line 25, reached in the payload-processing loop whose only index guard is '>= 0' (line 67); fx >= fc (e.g., fc == 1, fx == 1) passes the guard and stores through fp beyond the fc-element allocation of line 15.

Same heap OOB write (CWE-787) in the setmeta loop: guard at line 169 admits [0, INT_MAX], and fdata capacity is fc elements (line 15); fx == fc overruns the heap array and is written via fp (e.g., fp->stage at 177).

Same heap OOB write (CWE-787) in the commit loop: guard at line 183 admits [0, INT_MAX]; with fdata capacity fc (line 15), fx == fc indexes past the end and subsequent writes through fp (fp->stage at 195) corrupt the heap.

Same heap OOB write (CWE-787) in the backward-erase loop: guard at line 204 admits [0, INT_MAX]; fdata capacity is fc elements (line 15), so fx == fc is an out-of-bounds index whose struct fields (e.g., fp->stage read at 207, fp->fpath passed to fsmRemove at 214) are accessed/written past the allocation.

assumptions: fdata has exactly fc elements and valid indices 0..fc-1, from the declaration at line 15: 'struct filedata_s *fdata = xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata));'.
The fragment's only constraint on fx is the '>= 0' guard at the loop heads (lines 24, 67, 169, 183, 204); no statement in the fragment bounds fx above by fc or by any other constant.
xcalloc is treated as returning a valid allocation (no NULL-check semantics are shown for it).

callee-index consumers of the same unbounded fx — rpmfsGetAction(fs, fx) (line 29) and setFileState(fs, fx) (line 39) — may be equally OOB, but the capacity of fs is not identifiable from the fragment, so no separate finding.
Dereference of a NULL failedFile at lines 155, 176 and 197 is caller-dependent; the fragment does not establish that NULL can reach it.

Potential log injection through fp->fpath into rpmlog (lines 99–100): package-derived path bytes, including '\n', reach the log with no escaping shown; considered only low-impact log forgery and not reported as a CWE.
rc overwrite at line 37 by lines 43–44 can mask a failed rpmfiStat with a stale/zeroed fp->sb; downstream effect is a failing install, so no security impact confirmed.

rpmfilesIter/rpmfiNext NULL return and TOCTOU between fsmVerify (line 91) and fsmMkfile (line 111) are not confirmable from the fragment (framework pointer contracts and callee internals are outside the shown code).

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in unix_getpw: encrypted_pass is initialized to NULL (line 28), assigned from possibly-NULL library fields pwd->pw_passwd (line 46) or spwd->sp_pwdp (line 63), and dereferenced at line 137 without a NULL check. In builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM the only NULL guard in the fragment (line 59) is not compiled, so a User-Name resolving to an account with a NULL password field reaches encrypted_pass[0] as NULL and crashes the RADIUS server (remote DoS, CWE-476).

evidence.reason: CWE-476 NULL dereference. encrypted_pass has NULL in its residual range at this sink: it is initialized to NULL at line 28, assigned pwd->pw_passwd at line 46 (a library pointer the fragment never proves non-NULL; its own line-59 test `(encrypted_pass == NULL) || ...` and the lines 55-57 comment explicitly treat NULL password fields as possible), or spwd->sp_pwdp at line 63 with no NULL check. The line-59 guard is compiled only under #ifdef HAVE_GETSPNAM (lines 49-65); in builds where that block is absent, no statement between line 46 and line 137 constrains the value, so a request whose User-Name maps to an entry with pw_passwd == NULL passes every guard (line 23 username non-NULL, line 43 getpwnam non-NULL, shell/expiry checks untouched by encrypted_pass) and dereferences NULL at the sink, crashing the process.

assumptions: After the line 23-25 guard, request->username is non-NULL; this bound is established by the shown guard itself.

request->username->vp_strvalue is treated as a NUL-terminated string by %s, getpwnam, and getspnam; the fragment does not verify termination, so this is a framework-contract assumption, not a shown bound.

In builds where HAVE_GETSPNAM is undefined, the block at lines 49-65 (including the only NULL test on encrypted_pass, line 59) is not compiled; the fragment's #ifdef/#else structure makes this an explicitly possible configuration.

getpwnam/getspnam/getprpwnam results are NULL-checked (lines 31, 43, 60), so pwd/spwd/pr_pw are non-NULL wherever dereferenced; pw_passwd/pw_shell/sp_pwdp field nullability is not established by any shown statement except the fragment's own line-59 NULL test and the lines 55-57 comment.
limitations: The NULL deref witness depends on library/platform behavior (getpwnam returning pw_passwd == NULL, or sp_pwdp == NULL) and on the specific preprocessor configuration; the fragment demonstrates the NULL guard's necessity but does not itself instantiate a concrete NULL account, so confidence is capped at 0.55 (range-based, fragile-boundary finding).

Expiry arithmetic spwd->sp_lstchg + spwd->sp_max (line 107) could overflow only with shadow values near LONG_MAX; operands are system data, not attacker-directed, and the consequence is only a skipped reject — not a confirmed finding.

User-Name content flows unescaped into radlog/radlog_request %s arguments (lines 39, 77, 95, 108, 116, 127), so embedded newlines survive to the log (potential CWE-117 log injection); impact depends on unshown log consumers, so it is noted here rather than counted as an extra CWE.

verdict.summary: Unsigned (u32) overflow in the fsmeta accumulation (lines 9-13) lets an attacker-controlled on-disk superblock/checkpoint wrap the sum below `total`, defeating the `fsmeta >= total` layout check (line 15) and the minimum check (lines 21-22), so sanity_check_ckpt returns 0 (valid) for a corrupt image whose true fsmeta far exceeds total.

evidence.reason: All five addends are entry-point u32 reads (full 0..2^32-1 domain, no shown constraint before this block) accumulated into `unsigned int fsmeta` (line 3). C unsigned addition wraps mod 2^32. Witness: total=1000 (line 8), ckpt=0xFFFFFFFF, sit=0, nat=0, rsvd=501, ssa=0 gives true sum 4294967796 but wrapped fsmeta=500. Guard at line 15 admits 500 (500 < 1000), guards at lines 21-22 admit 500 (500 >= F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS for the assumed constant, ovp_segments=1 != 0, reserved_segments=501 != 0), so line 32 returns 0, accepting a layout whose true fsmeta exceeds total by ~4.29e9. The wrapped value is consumed by the comparison at line 15 that gates the accept/reject security decision: CWE-190.

assumptions: F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS is a fixed positive compile-time constant not defined in the fragment; the witness uses residue 500 and requires the constant to be <= 500 (any larger residue below the attacker-chosen total is equally reachable).
f2fs_cp_error(sbi) (line 28) returns false on the witness path; the fragment contains no statement setting or reading that flag, so the false outcome is assumed.
raw_super, ckpt, and sbi->sb are non-NULL on the shown path; the fragment contains no NULL-producing operation.
le32_to_cpu returns the stored u32 value (endianness conversion only).
limitations: The numeric value of F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS is not shown; the concrete example and the confidence depend on it being a small constant, though the wrap residue is fully attacker-controllable across [F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS, total-1].
f2fs_cp_error's state source is outside the fragment, so the accept path (line 32) cannot be proven from the shown code alone.
Downstream use of the accepted fsmeta/layout counts is not shown, so the ultimate memory-corruption impact of the validation bypass cannot be confirmed in this fragment.
No OOB, injection, NULL-deref, weak-crypto, or non-termination candidates were identified because the fragment contains no memory operations, format-string sinks, loops, or file/crypto operations.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the fragment. The loop at line 25 terminates in at most 17 iterations for all 16-bit `affectWhich` values. Remaining concerns (mis-swap of Bell/ActionMessage/CompatMap masks, dependence on `req_len` being in 4-byte words, unaligned access) are outside what the fragment can confirm.

assumptions: `client->req_len` is the request length in 4-byte words, as instantiated by the shown expression `dataLeft = (client->req_len * 4) - SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq)` at line 23.
`SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq)` is 16 bytes (2 CARD8 + 6 CARD16, consistent with the `swaps()` calls at lines 5-12), so `dataLeft ≡ 0 (mod 4)` initially and after every consumption of 4 or 8 bytes.
`REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE(xkbSelectEventsReq)` (line 6) rejects requests shorter than the fixed struct, giving `dataLeft ≥ 0` under the words reading of `req_len`.
`affectWhich`, `clear`, `selectAll` are 16-bit quantities (established by the `swaps()` byte-swap at lines 8-10), so `maskLeft` spans bits 0-15 and the loop terminates.
Event indices 12-15 reaching the `default:` case at line 49 return `BadValue` as a normal protocol error, not a reachable abort.
limitations: Size-1 events (XkbBellNotify/XkbActionMessage/XkbCompatMapNotify) are checked at line 53 for `dataLeft >= 2` but consume 4 bytes via `else { size = 2; }` at lines 63-67; this would underflow the unsigned `dataLeft` and overrun only if `dataLeft ≡ 2 (mod 4)`, which the fragment's own arithmetic at line 23 excludes. If the framework's `req_len` were in bytes rather than words, line 23 would over-read up to ~4x the region; that semantic is not visible in the fragment, so it can be neither confirmed nor ruled out here.

The size-1 path also omits byte-swapping of the 2-byte selection masks (lines 63-65 take no swap action), a correctness defect; its server-side impact would occur in the unshown `ProcXkbSelectEvents` (line 75) and cannot be confirmed from this fragment.

16/32-bit dereferences through the union at lines 56-61 may be unaligned; on strict-alignment architectures this is a potential SIGBUS DoS, but no memory-safety impact is demonstrated within the fragment.
`ErrorF` at line 70 passes unsigned `dataLeft` to `%d`; only a sign-mismatched printout, with no injection possible since the value is a numeric byte count.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled entry count from the stsz atom is read into int 'entries' at line 10 without validation and used at line 17 as the multiplicand of the allocation size 'entries * sizeof(long)'; the unsigned size_t product wraps on 32-bit targets (e.g., 0x40000001*4 == 4), yielding a tiny heap buffer whose NULL check at line 18 admits the small allocation, and the fill loop at lines 20-21 then writes 'entries' 4-byte samples out of bounds (heap overflow, CWE-787, root-cause integer overflow CWE-190).

evidence.reason: CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write. 'entries' (attacker-controlled uint32 read at line 10, stored in int with no shown validation; residual range includes all values 0..0x7FFFFFFF) drives both the loop bound at line 20 and the byte offset 4*i of this store. With sample_size==0 (admitted by the line 15 guard) and entries==0x40000001, line 17 computes entries*sizeof(long) in unsigned size_t: on a 32-bit target 1073741825*4 wraps to 4, so the allocation capacity is 4 bytes (offsets 0..3); the line 18 NULL check admits the non-NULL result. i=1 then writes at byte offset 4, already past capacity, and the loop continues to offset 2^32 — total 4294967296 bytes beyond the 4-byte buffer. The line-20 guard (i < entries) admits every such iteration, so the write's index is out of the sink's storage domain.

CWE-190 allocation-size integer overflow enabling the CWE-787 write. The size argument mixes signed int ('entries', line 10) with unsigned size_t ('sizeof(long)'); the int is converted to unsigned and the product is computed modulo 2^(8*sizeof(size_t)). For entries == 0x40000001 on a 32-bit size_t, 1073741825*4 wraps to 4 bytes, so av_malloc receives a capacity far smaller than the 'entries' 4-byte elements the loop at lines 20-21 writes into it. No shown statement constrains 'entries' before this computation.

assumptions: get_be32() returns an unsigned 32-bit big-endian value (standard ByteIOContext read); the assignment to int at line 10 yields the domain {0..0x7FFFFFFF} ∪ {-0x80000000..-1}.

The wrap witness assumes a target where sizeof(long)==4 and size_t is 32-bit (standard 32-bit ABI), the configuration in which the shown unsigned arithmetic wraps for positive int entries; on a 64-bit size_t the product cannot wrap for the admitted int range.
av_malloc(4) returns non-NULL when the heap can satisfy the request, which is the outcome the NULL check at line 18 admits.
limitations: Negative entries (uint32 values >= 0x80000000) make line 17 convert to a huge unsigned size; av_malloc then fails and line 19 returns -1 while the loop is skipped, so no in-fragment corruption results. The negative value is also stored to sc->sample_count at line 11, but downstream consumers are outside the fragment and unconfirmed.
Reads past the atom/file end at line 21 depend on get_be32 EOF behavior of ByteIOContext, which is not visible in the fragment.
Line 3 (c->fc->streams[c->fc->nb_streams-1]) would index -1 if nb_streams==0, but the nb_streams>=1 invariant is not shown in the fragment, so this is unconfirmable.

On 64-bit size_t targets, positive entries cannot wrap the multiplication and the loop writes exactly the allocated size, so the overflow does not occur there; resource exhaustion from a huge successful allocation is bounded within the fragment by the NULL check at line 18.

evidence.reason: argv[1] (entry-point input, line 29) passes the guards at line 25 (argc==2) and line 7 (non-NULL) with residual range "any NUL-terminated string of length n>=0", with no length bound in the fragment. strlen(str)=n at line 12 sizes the allocation to exactly n bytes (capacity quoted from `copy = (char *)malloc(strlen(str));` at line 12; valid indices 0..n-1). strcpy at line 16 writes n data bytes plus the terminating NUL, i.e., n+1 bytes, so the final write lands at index n == capacity, one byte past the end. Witness: argv[1]="a" -> strlen=1 -> malloc(1) capacity 1 -> strcpy writes 'a' at copy[0] and '\0' at copy[1]; the line 13 guard admits this path on malloc success. Primary CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write (off-by-one).

assumptions: argv[1] is a NUL-terminated string when argc==2 (C standard argv contract; relied on via the guard at line 25), so strlen/strcpy terminate.
strlen returns n = number of bytes before the NUL and strcpy therefore writes n+1 bytes; both are standard contracts of the shown calls.
The analyzed overflow path assumes malloc succeeds (guard at line 13 passes), which is the normal execution path for the sink.
The allocation at line 12 has exactly the requested size, so capacity = strlen(str) bytes.
Line numbers are counted from the rendered fragment: malloc at line 12, strcpy at line 16, argc guard at line 25, argv[1] assignment at line 29.
limitations: printf("%s", copy) at line 31 can receive NULL when malloc fails at line 12 (return path lines 13-14) or when strlen==0 and malloc(0) returns NULL; passing NULL to %s is UB but implementations commonly print "(null)", so this is an error-handling robustness concern with no confirmed security impact and is not reported as a finding.
The empty-string case still writes one byte past a zero-capacity allocation only if malloc(0) returns non-NULL; the non-empty witness "a" does not depend on this.
Severity assumes typical allocator behavior for a single NUL-byte heap overwrite; exact exploitable impact depends on allocator internals not shown.

malloc is used at line 12 while stdlib.h is included only later at line 22 (after my_strdup), making it an implicit declaration in C89 mode or a compile-time diagnostic in C99+; pointer-truncation risk is compiler-dependent and not confirmable from the fragment.
The argc!=2 branch at line 26 prints argv[0]; a NULL argv[0] there would be UB but requires conditions outside the shown code.
No secondary CWE is reported: the missing +1 in the size and the resulting one-byte overwrite constitute a single root cause (CWE-787).

If GC_init_lib_bounds() failed to set the bounds, a zeroed bounds state makes the range checks at lines 17-20 evaluate false and control falls through to REDIRECT_MALLOC — a benign fallback with no security-relevant failure state in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The stsz handler trusts the file-supplied `entries` count (L10) with only an integer-overflow guard (L11), so a crafted MOV can reach `av_malloc(entries * sizeof(long))` at L19 with up to ~4 GiB and drive the L22 loop for up to ~1.07e9 `get_be32` reads at L23 — no atom-size or resource cap exists in the fragment. A file with `sample_size=0` and `entries=1073741822` passes every guard (L11: 1073741822 < UINT_MAX/4) and triggers the unbounded allocation/iteration volume, a memory/CPU denial-of-service (CWE-770). The L11 guard does fully prevent integer overflow in the size arithmetic, so no memory-corruption CWE is confirmed.

verdict.summary: sanity_check_ckpt accumulates five attacker-controlled on-disk u32 segment counts (L11-L15) into a 32-bit unsigned int fsmeta. The corrupted value changes the security decision: a crafted superblock/checkpoint that should be rejected (return 1) is accepted (return 0), letting the mount validation proceed on an inconsistent layout.

The wrapped value is consumed by the security-gating comparisons at L17 (`if (fsmeta >= total)`) and L23 (`if (fsmeta < F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS ...)`) as an unsigned int, where the adversary sets total = K+2 so L17 admits K+1 < K+2 and L23 admits K+1 >= K, and the function returns 0 (accept) instead of the rejection the genuine sum would force. Success-path allocation amplification (up to 16*maxCutText bytes of decompressed allocations from a small compressed payload) is bounded and transient per message; sustained memory pressure from it depends on unshown rate limits and is recorded as a robustness concern only.

The confirmed leak's failure step depends on the unshown ZlibInStream exception behavior; if the reader instead returned short reads silently, the fragment would proceed with stale/partial data and the delete loop would still free the allocated entries - the concrete OOM witness requires the throw semantics noted in assumptions.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset allocates the response with g_malloc (line 14, no zeroing), writes only resp->hdr.type (line 15), then forwards the full sizeof(*resp)+max_size bytes to the guest (line 19). Bytes never written by any shown statement - including capset data not covered by the unguarded virgl_renderer_fill_caps call (lines 16-18) and any fields between hdr and capset_data - are transmitted uninitialized, disclosing host heap contents to the guest (CWE-457).

evidence.reason: Sink transmits sizeof(*resp)+max_size bytes starting at &resp->hdr, exactly the size of the g_malloc'd buffer at line 14, whose content is uninitialized except for resp->hdr.type (line 15) and the unshown write extent w of virgl_renderer_fill_caps (lines 16-18). max_size is admitted by the only guard (line 10) with residual range [1, 0xFFFFFFFF] and is never clamped or otherwise bounded; gc.capset_version (line 17) is guest-controlled and unvalidated against the fetched-but-unused max_ver (line 8). The fragment contains no statement initializing or zeroing the tail (no g_malloc0/memset, no fill-before-send guarantee, no w == max_size invariant), so uninitialized heap bytes reach the guest for any admitted capset_id/max_size - a confirmed use-of-uninitialized-memory information disclosure (CWE-457); confidence is capped because the exact uninitialized byte count depends on the unshown fill_caps contract.

assumptions: VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD(gc) at line 7 populates gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version from the guest-supplied command (macro body not shown).
gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version are uint32_t per the virtio-gpu ABI referenced by the fragment (struct definitions not shown).
glib g_malloc (line 14) returns uninitialized memory and aborts on allocation failure (standard glib semantics), which is why no NULL check is expected.
virtio_gpu_ctrl_response at line 19 delivers the given resp_len bytes to the guest device command queue.
limitations: The exact number of uninitialized bytes depends on the unshown write extent of virgl_renderer_fill_caps (lines 16-18); the finding is therefore a residual-range confirmation, not a single demonstrated byte (reflected in confidence 0.7).
The definition of struct virtio_gpu_resp_capset is not visible; any fields between hdr and capset_data are never written by shown statements, but their offsets cannot be computed from the fragment.

32-bit integer wrap of sizeof(*resp) + max_size (CWE-190/CWE-195) is not confirmable: it requires the host renderer to produce max_size near SIZE_MAX, which the fragment does not demonstrate; on LP64 the sum cannot wrap for the admitted uint32_t range.

A possible out-of-bounds write inside virgl_renderer_fill_caps caused by the unvalidated guest gc.capset_version (line 17) is unconfirmable (callee body not shown); the missing version check against the unused max_ver (line 8) is noted as a defensive gap only.
No findings for injection, crypto, file, authn/authz, or loop-termination classes: the fragment contains no such sinks and no loops.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in congratulate_user: the size argument passed to snprintf is 18 + userName_size + 1, derived entirely from the untrusted username length, instead of buffer_size. Since buffer is only char buffer[30] (30 bytes) at the call site, any username of 12 or more bytes makes snprintf write 31+ bytes into the 30-byte stack buffer (e.g., a 13-byte argv[1] writes 32 bytes, 2 past the end).

evidence.reason: snprintf writes up to (18 + userName_size + 1) bytes (size-1 chars plus NUL) into buffer, whose only visible capacity is char buffer[30] at line 27. userName_size is entry-point input derived as strlen(argv[1]) at line 28, unconstrained by any shown check (line 21's argc != 2 guard only ensures argv[1] exists). The format literal is 17 + strlen(userName) + 1 characters plus NUL, so the full string is written. For userName_size >= 12 the size argument (>= 31) exceeds the 30-byte capacity and snprintf writes past index 29; concrete witness: argv[1] = "abcdefghijklm" (13 chars) passes the argc == 2 guard, gives userName_size = 13, size argument 32, and writes 32 bytes (2-byte OOB write, NUL at index 31). The dead parameter buffer_size (value 30 at the call site, line 28) is never used, so the input-derived size is the confirmed root cause: CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow.

assumptions: Destination capacity is char buffer[30] at line 27, giving writable indices 0..29.
argc == 2 (guard at line 21) guarantees argv[1] is a valid, NUL-terminated string but imposes no length bound.
userName_size equals strlen(argv[1]) at the call site (line 28), so it equals the byte length of userName.
The format literal contributes 17 bytes ("Congratulations, ") + 1 byte ("!") + 1 NUL, so the complete output is userName_size + 19 bytes.
limitations: Integer overflow of 18 + userName_size + 1 requires userName_size near INT_MAX (only conceivable if strlen(argv[1]) exceeded INT_MAX before the int conversion) and is not an independent root cause since the overflow already triggers at length 12.
The discarded snprintf return value (line 15) is not consumed by any later security-relevant operation, so no error-handling flaw is confirmed.
buffer_size is documented as the buffer size but is never used in the function body; this is the same root cause as the overflow, not a separate CWE.

verdict.summary: In the mb_ereg_replace replacement loop, the per-character byte width fwd returned by php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex() (line 86) is passed unclamped as the length of out_buf.append(p, fwd) (line 101). The only guard on this path, while (i < replacement.size()) (line 85), bounds the starting offset but never bounds fwd by the remaining replacement bytes, so a multi-byte character lead byte at the end of the attacker-supplied replacement makes append() read fwd - (replacement.size() - i) bytes past the end of the valid substitution region — a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Sink at line 101 passes fwd (derived at line 86 from php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex(p, enc), residual range unconstrained — no shown statement bounds it) as the length of StringBuffer::append. The loop guard at line 85 admits i = replacement.size()-1 (e.g., i = 0 for a 1-byte replacement), and the backref guard at lines 88-89 is bypassed for fwd != 1, routing execution to the else branch. For a multi-byte encoding whose lead byte at the final position reports a width fwd > replacement.size() - i, append reads fwd bytes from replacement.data() + i, i.e. fwd - (replacement.size() - i) bytes past the valid region [data(), data()+size()) that the code itself uses at line 85 — heap out-of-bounds read, CWE-125. No statement between lines 86 and 101 clamps fwd to the remaining bytes.

assumptions: str.size() (line 61) and replacement.size() (line 85) define byte-length valid regions [data(), data()+size()) for each String.
enc is non-null on every reaching path because of the guard at lines 21-22.
The eval option (line 30, parsed from option) cannot lead to code execution because eval is checked at lines 54-56 and throws.

On match, onig_search supplies group-0 offsets used at lines 80-81 and 106-108; the fragment's own backref guard at lines 93-94 shows offsets are not universally trusted, so paths relying on the unshown oniguruma contract are treated as unestablished.
limitations: The exact excess at the line 101 sink depends on the active encoding's character-width semantics inside php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex (callee not shown); the out-of-domain length (unclamped fwd) is established by the shown code, the byte count is a library-range claim.
Potential negative-length append at lines 80-81 requires regs->beg[0] < pos - str.data(), which depends on the unshown oniguruma region contract — not confirmed.
If oniguruma ever reported end[0] > str.size(), pos could advance past string_lim at line 108; unconfirmed from the fragment.
onig_region_new() (line 62) is unchecked; a NULL regs would only arise on allocation failure and be dereferenced inside the library — no confirmed security-relevant operation on the failure state.
fwd == 0 would stall the replacement loop (lines 103/85); the callee's production of 0 is not shown — non-termination unconfirmed.
Discarded returns of onig_error_code_to_str (line 68) and _php_mb_regex_init_options (line 30) have no shown security-relevant consequence.
ReDoS/backtracking behavior of oniguruma is library-internal and not analyzable from the fragment.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmed within the shown fragment. The only termination sink, pcmk_panic (line 34), is gated solely by the operator-controlled PCMK_fail_fast environment flag and is the documented fail-fast behavior of the code (comments at lines 7-10, log at line 33); its witness also depends on the unshown crm_is_true contract and on an environment trust boundary not visible in the fragment. Every other candidate - respawn_count overflow (line 17), log injection via child fields, NULL dereference, discarded return statuses, and the partial pcmk_child_active comparison - depends on types, capacities, field provenance, or callee contracts that are not declared in the shown code, so no CWE can be substantiated.

assumptions: The fragment contains no loops and no buffer declarations, allocations, copies, or length/size computations, so no object capacity exists within the shown code for OOB or boundary claims.
child is an internal-helper parameter; the fragment neither produces NULL nor establishes a non-NULL contract for it.
All format strings passed to the crm_* loggers are string literals, so CWE-134 format-string injection does not apply.
limitations: C1 (reachable abort, lines 32-34): pcmk_panic is reached when crm_is_true(getenv("PCMK_fail_fast")) is nonzero; this is the code's intended fail-fast reboot behavior (comments lines 7-10, log line 33). The daemon's environment trust boundary is not established in the fragment, and the exact admissible env string depends on the unshown crm_is_true contract, so no concrete witness can be demonstrated; treated as a design/hardening concern, not a confirmed finding (no CWE).

C2 (respawn_count overflow, lines 17-18, sink at line 50): the declared type of respawn_count and the type/value of MAX_RESPAWN are not shown, so a wrap that would make line 18 false and allow unbounded respawning cannot be grounded; CWE-190/CWE-400 unconfirmable.

C3 (log injection, lines 19, 33, 37-39, 49): provenance of child->name and child->endpoint is unshown and the escaping behavior of the crm_* loggers is not visible; CWE-117 unconfirmable. String NUL-termination for the %s reads is likewise not established in the fragment.
C4 (NULL dereference, lines 4-5): no operation in the shown code produces NULL; a NULL child could only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller, which is a limitation, not a finding (CWE-476).

C5 (unchecked returns, lines 15, 23-25, 27, 44-45, 50): update_node_processes, mainloop_set_trigger, g_timeout_add_seconds, and start_child return values are discarded, but no callee contract is shown and no security-relevant operation runs on a failure state, so CWE-754/390 is not confirmed.

C6 (partial outcome comparison, line 36): pcmk_child_active(child) == 1 admits only exactly 1; any other value (including a possible error) falls through to start_child (line 50), but the callee's return domain is not shown, so error-mishandling is unconfirmable.

C7 (line 15, 27): a NULL result from get_process_list() forwarded to update_node_processes with the status discarded cannot be confirmed as a flaw because neither callee's contract nor a failure consumer is visible in the fragment.

verdict.summary: The fragment implements PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password hashing with per-password 32-byte salts from RAND_bytes. Within the shown program, all array indexing is in-bounds: count is derived from argc (>=3), passwords is sized exactly count (line 57) and fully populated (lines 60-63), and the hashing loop (line 23) reads indices 0..count-1. Both RAND_bytes and PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC return values are checked before exit. No attacker-controlled value reaches an out-of-domain index, size, format string, or unguarded abort, so no vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code.

assumptions: main's guard `if (argc < 3)` (line 50) admits only argc >= 3, so `count = (argc - 1) / 2` (line 55) is >= 1.
`std::vector<std::string> passwords(count)` (line 57) gives passwords.size() == count, and lines 60-63 assign every element before the call at line 65.
`2 * count <= argc - 1` follows from integer floor division at line 55, so the max argv index `2 + 2*(count-1)` (line 62) is a valid argv index.
salt and hash vectors are fixed at 32 bytes (lines 25-26), matching the SHA-256 output size used at line 35.
limitations: If hash_passwords were called by an unseen caller with count > passwords.size(), `passwords[i]` at line 35 would be an out-of-bounds read; no such call path exists in the shown fragment (the only caller, main, guarantees size == count), so this is not a confirmed finding and carries no CWE.

`passwords[i].length()` (size_t) is narrowed to the `int passlen` parameter of PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC at line 35; a >INT_MAX-length input would corrupt passlen, but no shown code can produce such a string and the corrupted length would not overflow the fixed 32-byte output buffer, so the impact is unconfirmed.

The 10,000-iteration PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 configuration is below current OWASP guidance for password storage; the code implements the parameters explicitly required by the specification comment, so it is a hardening note rather than a code-selected weakness, and no CWE is attached.
`count` passed to `result.reserve(count)` (line 21) would only be negative for an out-of-fragment caller; at the shown call site count >= 1, so no reachable exception path exists.
The `usernames` parameter is unused in hash_passwords; this is a code-quality issue, not a security vulnerability.

The callee getFieldAt and its return/error behavior are not shown, so the effect of J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL on a failed resolution cannot be further analyzed; no security-relevant operation in the fragment consumes a failure state.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability: the fragment contains scalar timestamp arithmetic and constant-format logging only. No memory, injection, crypto, file, or control-flow sink is present, and every plausible issue (uninitialized num/den after an unchecked compute_frame_duration call, int64 negation overflow at line 27, zero time_base.num reaching av_rescale, and %Ld/int64_t varargs mismatch) either depends on callee behavior outside the fragment or corrupts only timestamp data with no security-relevant downstream use.

AV_NOPTS_VALUE, AV_TIME_BASE, FFMAX, CODEC_TYPE_AUDIO/VIDEO are constants/enumerators whose bodies are outside the fragment; their use here is comparison/sentinel and constant-multiplication only.
