Sink: identical unbounded %s write into char dr[10] (declaration at line 105) after the non-NULL guard at 103. The same argv-derived optarg ('-f' argument), e.g. 10 bytes with no whitespace, writes 11 bytes into a 10-byte buffer. The sscanf return check afterwards cannot constrain the already-performed store. CWE-121.

Sink: identical unbounded %s write into char dr[10] (declaration at line 119) after the non-NULL guard at 117. '-b' option argument of >=10 bytes (e.g., "1111111111") writes past dr by >=1 byte; no width in the format string and no length check on optarg anywhere in the fragment. CWE-121.

Sink: identical unbounded %s write into char dr[10] (declaration at line 133) after the non-NULL guard at 131. '-l' option argument of >=10 bytes (e.g., "1111111111") writes 11 bytes into a 10-byte buffer, overflowing adjacent stack locals and, for longer tokens, the saved return address. CWE-121.

assumptions: argv and optarg are NUL-terminated C strings supplied by the runtime/getopt_long (standard libc/OS contract); the fragment itself imposes only the non-NULL guard on optarg and never constrains its length.

file_ext is an external array whose element count/capacity is not visible in the fragment; format is confined to {1,2} at the file_ext[format] index sites (111-112 plus the showHelp early return at 193-197), but no capacity is identifiable for a boundary claim.
LC/MAIN/LTP/LD, FAAD_FMT_16BIT, FIXED_POINT_CAP, FAAD2_VERSION, and file_ext are declared outside the fragment and are treated as opaque.
limitations: fread return at line 263 is discarded; for inputs shorter than 8 bytes header[4..7] (declared at line 22) is partially/fully uninitialized and is consumed at 268 and pushed back at 278-285. This is a real uninitialized-read/error-handling concern (CWE-390/CWE-457 flavor) but the downstream operations have no confirmed memory-safety or injection impact, so it is demoted.

Eight ungetc calls (278-285) exceed the C-standard guaranteed minimum of one pushback; portability/robustness issue with no memory-safety impact, and all indices (header[0..7]) are in bounds of header[8].

Allocation-size arithmetic at line 227 (strlen(aacFileName) + strlen(file_ext[format]) + 1) cannot be audited for integer wrap because file_ext's element strings/capacity are not shown; the copies at 233/240 are byte-exact against that allocation.
format/object_type/outputFormat range checks (111-112, 139-145, 125-126) feed decode functions whose parsing behavior is outside the fragment; no finding is asserted for those callees.

verdict.summary: pktRemoveEvidence reads argv[0] at line 6 without validating the argument list (argc is never used and no argv.size()/isEmpty() check exists). A packet invoking this handler with an empty argument list indexes a zero-element QStringList at index 0 — an out-of-bounds read of one QString element (undefined behavior in release builds; Q_ASSERT abort in debug builds). CWE-125.

evidence.reason: argv (declared `QStringList argv` at line 1) is entry-point input whose full declared domain includes the empty list; the fragment imposes no constraint before line 6 (argc is unused; no argv.size()/isEmpty() check), so the empty witness passes every guard on the path (there is none upstream of the sink; line 7's is_int check occurs after the access and binds only parse success, not list length). `argv[0]` is the standard indexed element access whose contract is 0 <= i < size(); for the empty witness, index 0 == capacity 0, i.e., an out-of-bounds read of one QString element (excess = 1 element; CWE-125). The call site is out-of-domain for the admitted input: Qt's release build performs the raw element fetch (UB), and debug builds abort via Q_ASSERT.

assumptions: argv's role is entry-point input: line 1 declares it as a packet-handler parameter, and no shown statement constrains its length before line 6, so the empty list (size 0) remains a member of its declared domain.

For the deleteEvidence sink at line 8 the capacity is area->evidence().size() as evaluated at line 7; the guard admits only 0 <= idx < size(), so idx == size() (the only off-by-one hazard) is excluded by the strict < comparison.
limitations: Reachability of the empty-argv witness depends on an unshown packet dispatcher invoking this handler with zero arguments; the fragment shows no caller and establishes no minimum argv length, which caps confidence at 0.6.

The exact release-build behavior of QStringList::operator[] out of range (raw out-of-bounds read) and its debug-build Q_ASSERT are Qt implementation details not visible in the fragment; the finding relies on the container's standard documented index contract (0 <= i < size()).
No NULL-deref finding for area is confirmed: no shown statement can produce a NULL AreaData*.
The idx/deleteEvidence path is fully protected by line 7; no other memory-safety, injection, crypto, or file-handling sinks exist in the fragment.

verdict.summary: A crafted tar archive can write files outside dest_path because path safety only rejects leading-'/' and '..' components (is_path_safe, lines 172/180) and never inspects entry type or link targets: a symlink entry "link" -> /etc followed by "link/passwd" is extracted through the link (line 144 creates the link, line 157 writes through it), giving arbitrary file write as the extracting process user (CWE-59). Additionally, pass 2 never re-runs is_path_safe and re-opens the archive by name after pass 1 (lines 125-130), so a file swapped between the two passes extracts unvalidated paths (CWE-367).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled archive pathname flows from archive_entry_pathname(entry) (line 138) into full_path via snprintf (line 140) and archive_entry_set_pathname (line 142); write_data_block writes through the OS-resolved path. Entry "link/passwd" passes guards at 172 (first char 'l') and 180 (tokens {"link","passwd"}) in pass 1, then line 144 previously created symlink dest/link -> /etc (entry type and link target are never checked; flags at line 78 set only ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME|ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM, so no SECURE_SYMLINKS protection at line 103). The write at this sink lands at /etc/passwd via the link — CWE-59 arbitrary file creation/overwrite outside dest_path.

Same taint path (lines 138-142). This call materializes the attacker-named object at full_path; for symlink entry "link" (admitted by guards 172/180) it creates dest/link -> /etc, and for subsequent entries the OS resolves dest/link as a path component during header/data writes, enabling the CWE-59 write outside dest_path.

current_file at line 138 comes from a second, independent open of tar_path at line 130, after archive_read_free at line 125; the only path-safety guard, is_path_safe at line 116, ran on the FIRST read (opened at line 107) and is absent from the second-pass loop (137-144). If the file is replaced between the two passes, a name such as "../x" or "/etc/x" reaches this path construction and the extraction sinks unvalidated — CWE-367 check-then-use on a re-opened resource, with arbitrary-write impact; requires the race interleaving, so the claim is capped at confidence 0.8.

assumptions: PATH_MAX is 512 (line 11) and full_path is char full_path[PATH_MAX] (line 139); snprintf(full_path, PATH_MAX, ...) at line 140 is bounded to 511 chars + NUL, so no buffer overflow — only silent truncation.
archive_entry_pathname() results are treated as non-NULL (no nullable contract visible in the fragment), so the dereference at is_path_safe line 172 is not counted as a NULL-deref finding.

libarchive disk-writer semantics: write_header creates symlinks/hardlinks for link-type entries and the OS resolves symlink components of later write paths when ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS is not set; the shown flags (line 78) and options call (line 103) do not set it.
The archive read from argv[1] is attacker-influenced data; every pathname/entry it yields is entry-point input.
limitations: CWE-367 witness requires an external modification of tar_path between the two opens (lines 125 and 130); the diverging file content is not producible by the fragment alone, so it is the secondary finding with confidence capped at 0.8.

Error-handling flaw (demoted): the non-OK return of archive_read_data_block at line 156 is discarded; line 168 can return true after a partial/failed data extraction, contradicting the contract at lines 14-15. Exact 'headers still reach ARCHIVE_EOF after a data error' outcome depends on libarchive continuation semantics not visible in the fragment.
is_path_safe could crash via strtok(NULL, ...) at line 177 if strdup at line 176 fails (OOM); unchecked allocation with only a DoS outcome is not a confirmed finding.
snprintf truncation at line 140 can cause path collisions and partial extraction for very long dest_path/name concatenations; silent truncation with no confirmed security impact.
Empty or '.' pathnames are admitted by is_path_safe and could alter dest metadata via ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME/PERM; impact unconfirmed.
No memory-safety finding: the only size-like value feeding a sink is the constant 512 bound of snprintf (lines 11/139/140); buff/size/offset at line 157 are library-provided and forwarded unmodified.

verdict.summary: In the success path, *length is assigned the signed pointer difference file->buffer - file->limit (line 8). No shown statement constrains the relative order of buffer and limit, so the residual range includes negative differences; converting a negative difference to size_t wraps it to a huge value (e.g., SIZE_MAX for -1), corrupting the length returned to callers, which is consumed as the size of the returned buffer and enables out-of-bounds reads. Root cause: signed-to-unsigned conversion of a negative value (CWE-195).

evidence.reason: The size_t out-parameter is assigned file->buffer - file->limit, which has type ptrdiff_t (signed). The guard at line 2 admits only backend == &mem_backend, and the guard at line 7 admits only length != NULL; neither constrains the ordering of file->buffer and file->limit, so the residual range of the difference includes negative values (e.g., -1 when limit points one byte past buffer). The signed-to-unsigned conversion at line 8 wraps a negative difference to a huge size_t (SIZE_MAX on 64-bit for -1), so the length returned to callers does not match the returned buffer's actual size and is consumed as if in-domain, enabling out-of-bounds reads in any caller that reads *length bytes — CWE-195.

assumptions: file->backend, file->buffer, and file->limit are readable members of hFILE once the function is entered (dereferenced at lines 2, 8, and 10 without further validation).
length, when non-NULL, is a writable size_t*; the only constraint the shown code applies is the NULL check at line 7.

Under C semantics, buffer - limit has type ptrdiff_t (signed), and assignment to size_t converts negative values modulo 2^N; no statement in the fragment constrains the relative order of buffer and limit.
limitations: The negative-difference witness (buffer < limit) rests on the residual range of unconstrained pointer members; the mem backend's internal data layout is not visible in the fragment, so the exact value cannot be derived from fragment-internal state — this caps confidence at 0.7.
A NULL file pointer would crash at lines 2/8/10, but NULL cannot be produced inside the shown code; only an out-of-scope caller could supply it, so it is not a finding.
The downstream consumer of *length is not shown; the resulting out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) cannot be capacity-grounded in this fragment and is recorded as a limitation rather than a separate CWE.
No other memory-safety, injection, crypto, file-handling, concurrency, or reachable-abort candidates are present in the fragment.

verdict.summary: The command-line frontend performs several unbounded copies of attacker-controlled argv data into fixed stack buffers: width-less sscanf("%s") writes arbitrarily long -s/-f/-b/-l option strings into 10-byte char dr[10] buffers (lines 83, 94, 108, 122), and raw strcpy() writes -o, -a, and positional arguments into 255-byte buffers (lines 69, 76, 196). All are reachable with concrete argv lengths (10 and 255 bytes respectively), none is length-guarded anywhere in the shown code, and the option-loop overflows occur before the showHelp early return. These are stack buffer overflows (CWE-121) that corrupt memory and may enable code execution.

evidence.reason: optarg is entry-point input with no length constraint in the shown code; the width-less %s at line 83 writes token+1 bytes into char dr[10] (declared at line 82, capacity 10). Witness: -s 1234567890 (10 chars) writes 11 bytes, overflowing by 1 byte at index 10. The sscanf(...) < 1 test runs after the write and cannot prevent it; the if (optarg) guard at line 80 admits it. Stack-based buffer overflow, primary CWE-121.

Same pattern as line 83: width-less %s writes an unbounded token plus NUL into char dr[10] (line 93). Witness: -f with a 10-char token writes 11 bytes into a 10-byte buffer (1-byte stack overflow). Guard at line 91 (optarg non-NULL) admits it. CWE-121.
Same pattern: width-less %s into char dr[10] (line 107); a 10-char -b argument overflows by 1 byte. Guard at line 105 admits any non-NULL optarg. CWE-121.
Same pattern: width-less %s into char dr[10] (line 121); a 10-char -l argument overflows by 1 byte. Guard at line 119 admits any non-NULL optarg. CWE-121.

Entry-point optarg (unconstrained length) is copied into char audioFileName[255] (declared at line 20). Witness: -o with 255 chars writes 256 bytes (chars 0..254 + NUL at 255), overflowing the 255-byte buffer by 1 byte; the guard if (optarg) at line 66 admits it. The copy executes inside the option loop, before the early-return check at lines 181-185, so no later guard protects it. Unbounded stack copy, CWE-121.

Entry-point optarg is copied into char adtsFileName[255] (declared at line 21). Witness: -a with 255 chars writes 256 bytes, overflowing by 1 byte; guard at line 73 admits it, and the copy precedes the line 181 early return. Unbounded stack copy, CWE-121.

Entry-point positional argument argv[optind] is copied into char aacFileName[255] (declared at line 19) with no length check. The guard at line 181 only ensures argc - optind >= 1 (existence of the argument) and does not bound its length. Witness: a 255-char positional argument writes 256 bytes, overflowing by 1 byte. Unbounded stack copy, CWE-121.

assumptions: Destination capacities are fixed by the visible declarations: char aacFileName[255] (line 19), char audioFileName[255] (line 20), char adtsFileName[255] (line 21), char dr[10] (lines 82, 93, 107, 121), unsigned char header[8] (line 22).

getopt_long supplies a non-NULL optarg when an argument-requiring option is given; the fragment's if (optarg) guards (lines 66, 73, 80, 91, 105, 119) are consistent with that contract, and the witnesses pass them.
The option loop terminates because getopt_long returns -1, which breaks the while(1) loop at lines 58-62.
limitations: strcat(audioFileName, file_ext[format]) at line 216 is not evidenced: file_ext is not declared or valued in the fragment, so the appended length and the exact overflow boundary (total > 255) cannot be concretely witnessed from the shown code alone.
strcpy(audioFileName, aacFileName) at line 209 duplicates the line 196 sink with the same threshold (strlen >= 255); line 196 corrupts first, so it is not separately evidenced.

fread at line 239 has its return status discarded; on inputs shorter than 8 bytes, header[4..7] may be uninitialized when read at line 244 and pushed back at lines 254-261, but the fragment shows only a decode-path branch effect with no confirmed security-relevant harm (demoted error/status-handling candidate).
def_srate (line 86) accepts any atoi() output and is consumed only by the unshown decodeAACfile, so no in-domain violation is derivable.
The capacity of file_ext is not shown; format is confined to {1,2} by lines 99-100 plus the early return at 181-185, but whether index 2 is in-bounds is unconfirmable.
Float division by a possibly zero dec_length at lines 280-281 is not treated as a security finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The four feed-controlled fields (url, title, description, feed_title) are each passed through utils::replace_all(...,"'","%27") at lines 12-15 and embedded inside single-quote segments by the constant format literal at line 10; /bin/sh -c (lines 27-31) terminates a single-quoted segment only at a quote byte, and no field can contain one after the replacement, so shell metacharacters cannot escape their quoting on the non-interactive path (and the identical cmdline is used on the interactive path at line 22). bookmark_cmd is executed unquoted as configured, which is the intended operator-controlled behavior. Remaining concerns (newline survival into a DEBUG log, embedded-NUL truncation) have no demonstrated security impact and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: POSIX sh single-quote semantics apply to the visible "/bin/sh" + "-c" invocation at lines 27-28: a segment delimited by ' ends only at the next ' byte, and all other bytes inside it (including $, ;, |, backticks, backslash, newline) are literal.
The replacement at lines 12-15 is applied to each field BEFORE strprintf::fmt embeds it at line 10, so no single quote can appear inside the quoted segments of cmdline.
cmdline is a std::string with dynamic storage (declared line 10); its concatenation is exact and no fixed-size buffer capacity exists in the fragment, so no memory-capacity arithmetic applies.
utils::run_interactively at line 22 executes the command string through a shell; its body is not shown, so this is name-implied, and the single-quote protection relies on shell-family semantics.

Config values (lines 7-8), including bookmark-cmd executed as a command, are operator-supplied by design; a malicious config is the operator attacking themselves, not a boundary crossing in the fragment.
limitations: Command injection via url/title/description/feed_title (CWE-78 candidate): taint reaches the sinks at lines 22 and 29-31, but no witness can be constructed — every field has all ' bytes removed at lines 12-15 and is wrapped in '...' at line 10, so no field can close its quote under /bin/sh semantics; a simulated payload "'; rm -rf ~; '" becomes the single literal argument "%27; rm -rf ~; %27".

Log injection (CWE-117 candidate) at line 17: newline bytes survive replacement and reach the DEBUG log, enabling forged debug entries; demoted because the fragment shows no security-relevant consumer of this log.

Embedded NUL in any field would truncate cmdline at line 29's c_str(); the pre-NUL prefix is quote-constrained and the post-NUL bytes are dropped, so the worst case is a shell syntax error, not injection; demoted.

The interactive-path executor (line 22) is not shown; if it invoked a non-POSIX interpreter that decodes %27 or treats single quotes differently, the safe conclusion for that branch would need revisiting.
bookmark_cmd (line 7) is concatenated unquoted at line 11 and executed as the command; this is the intended configuration feature and is not treated as attacker-controlled within the fragment.

verdict.summary: The precinct index prcno computed at line 81 (prcvind*numhprcs+prchind, where prchind grows with the x-loop value) can equal or exceed numprcs for geometry admitted by every shown guard; the only in-fragment protection is assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs) at line 83. For state numrlvls=1, expn=0, hsamp=vsamp=1, xend=2, numhprcs=1, numprcs=1, x=1 gives prchind=1 and prcno=1, so the assert fails (CWE-617 reachable abort, DoS in assert-enabled builds); with asserts compiled out the same out-of-domain index reaches prclyrnos at line 87 (the known heap-overflow path, though the array capacity is not declared in this fragment). Independently, sampling factors vsamp/hsamp are never validated: vsamp==0 makes the JPC_CEILDIV at line 68 and the modulo at line 50 divide by zero, also a crash (CWE-369).

evidence.reason: CWE-617. prcno (line 81) = prcvind*numhprcs+prchind; prchind (lines 75-77) = FLOORDIVPOW2(CEILDIV(x, hsamp<<r), prcwidthexpn) - FLOORDIVPOW2(trx0, prcwidthexpn). Witness admitted by every shown guard: numrlvls=1, prcwidthexpn=prcheightexpn=0, hsamp=vsamp=1, xstart=ystart=0, xend=2, yend=1, numhprcs=1, numprcs=1, x=1, y=0. Exponent guard (30-33) admits 0+1=1<=NUMBITS-2; L57 admits rlvlno=0<numrlvls=1; L61 admits numprcs=1!=0; alignment gate (69-74) admits x%1==0 and y%1==0; prchind=1, prcno=1, so assert(1<1) fails. The assert is the only statement bounding prcno, and the failing value is derived entirely from unvalidated pi geometry, so the abort is attacker-directed; in NDEBUG builds the same prcno is used as the index into prclyrnos at line 87 (capacity not shown, see limitations).

CWE-369. picomp->vsamp is not constrained by any shown check (type not visible in the fragment; 0 belongs to every integer domain), and r = numrlvls-1-rlvlno >= 0 by the L57 guard, so vsamp<<r == 0 when vsamp==0. JPC_CEILDIV divides by its second argument, so the denominator 0 causes integer division by zero (SIGFPE) before any alignment check. Guards on the path (L30-33 exponent bound, L57 rlvlno<numrlvls, L61 numprcs!=0, L55-56 compno bounds, L49/L51 loop entry) all admit the state; witness: vsamp=0, numrlvls=1, rlvlno=0, ystart=0<yend=1.

CWE-369, same root cause as the line-68 sink. pi->ystep becomes 0 when picomp->vsamp==0 via lines 38-41 (ystep = vsamp * 2^exp) with no nonzero check; with ystart<yend the y-loop body executes and its first update evaluates pi->y % pi->ystep with divisor 0, a division-by-zero crash. The symmetric x-loop update at line 52 divides by pi->xstep, which is 0 when hsamp==0 (lines 36-37, 40); a negative step (unsigned wrap at L38-39 assigned to int) would make the L49 condition y<yend never flip, i.e. non-termination.

assumptions: JPC_CEILDIV(a,b) performs ceiling division by b and JPC_FLOORDIVPOW2(a,b) performs floor division by 2^b, per their names and the divisor/exponent arguments the shown code passes; only that standard semantics is used.

The fields of pi (jpc_pi_t) are packet-iterator state populated by the caller from JPEG 2000 codestream parameters (component sampling factors, precinct width/height exponents, progression-change ranges); the fragment itself imposes only the constraints audited in Phase 1.
uint_fast32_t has at least 32 bits, so JAS_UINTFAST32_NUMBITS-2 >= 30 and the exponent guard at lines 30-33 admits the witnesses used (exponent sum = 1).
numprcs is the intended upper bound for prcno, as stated by the assert at line 83, with prclyrnos expected to hold numprcs entries; this is the fragment's only statement about that bound.
limitations: Heap OOB read/write of pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos[pi->prcno] at line 87 (read at 88, write at 89) is not reported as its own CWE because the capacity of prclyrnos is not identifiable from the fragment (no declaration/allocation visible); per CAPACITY GROUNDING the index == numprcs boundary claim is unconfirmable here, although the assert's invariant and the known CVE-2016-9580 pattern point to the same root cause.

Negative or out-of-range starts (pchg->rlvlnostart < 0, pchg->compnostart < 0 or >= numcomps) can form &pi->picomps[pi->compno] (line 54) and index pi->picomp->pirlvls[pi->rlvlno] (line 60) out of bounds; the capacities of picomps/pirlvls are not shown, so those OOB claims are unconfirmable.
int overflow of prcno = prcvind*numhprcs+prchind (line 81) could corrupt the index and the assert comparison, but demonstrating the consequence needs array capacities not shown in the fragment.
Whether assertions are enabled (NDEBUG) in the target build is not shown; with asserts disabled line 83 is a no-op and the out-of-domain prcno reaches line 87 directly.
JPEG 2000 requires sampling factors >= 1, but that invariant is outside this fragment and is not used in either direction; the fragment contains no such check.
The goto skip continuation (lines 20-21, 92-93) relies on prior-call values of pi->rlvlno/y/x/compno/lyrno; no in-fragment invariant violation was demonstrated for it.
No injection, crypto, file, or authn/authz sinks exist in the shown code; no such findings are reported.

verdict.summary: The FORMAT_INT precision zero-pad (lines 204-207) writes an attacker-controlled precision count of bytes downward from workend into the fixed stack buffer `char work[BUFFSIZE]` with no shown upper bound on `prec` (only a negative-to-1 default at lines 187-188 and the FLAGS_PREC/FLAGS_PRECPARAM pickups at lines 118-130). A format such as `%.2147483647d` drives `prec` to LONG_MAX-1, writing ~2^31 bytes below `work[0]` (CWE-787 stack out-of-bounds write, followed by an out-of-bounds read at lines 240-242).

evidence.reason: Precision `prec` (long, line 50) is taken from entry-point format/argument data via `prec = p->precision;` (line 128) or `prec = (long)vto[p->precision].data.num.as_signed;` (line 119) with no shown cap (lines 122-125 only map negative to -1; lines 187-188 only set a default). After line 197 (`prec -= (long)(workend - w);`) the residual equals the supplied precision minus digit count; for witness format `%.2147483647d` with value 5, residual = 2147483646. The guard `if(prec > 0)` (line 204) admits the entire positive range, so the loop at line 206 executes 2147483646 times and this statement writes 2147483646 bytes descending from `&work[BUFFSIZE-3]` (w initialized at line 191 from `workend = &work[sizeof(work)-2]`, line 32), exceeding the declared capacity `char work[BUFFSIZE];` (line 25) by 2147483646-(BUFFSIZE-2) bytes — a stack OOB write (CWE-787) with attacker-controlled write count.

assumptions: `format` is NUL-terminated, as relied on by `while(*f != '\0')` (line 42) and `strlen(str)` (line 273).

`dprintf_Pass1` (line 35) populates `vto`, `endpos` and its return is checked (line 36); its body is outside the fragment, so fields it stores (e.g., `p->precision`) retain full declared-type domains.
`char work[BUFFSIZE]` (line 25) is a fixed-size stack object of BUFFSIZE bytes; the numeric value of the named constant BUFFSIZE is defined outside the fragment.
`OUTCHAR` (used throughout, e.g., line 70) is a macro defined outside the fragment; per the comment (lines 2-4) it emits one character through `stream` and its return value is intentionally unused.
limitations: The exact byte excess of the confirmed CWE-787 write depends on the unshown numeric value of BUFFSIZE; the write count (2^31-ish) is fully established in the fragment, and the finding assumes BUFFSIZE < 2^31, which caps confidence at 0.75.

`p = &vto[param]` (line 99) and the `endpos` walk `f = *end++;` (line 421) could index out of bounds for oversized `%<n>$` positional specs or oversized spec counts, but the capacities `vto[MAX_PARAMETERS]`/`endpos[MAX_PARAMETERS]` (lines 21-22) have unshown constants and Pass1 (line 35) validation is not shown — boundary unconfirmable.

`(sprintf)(work, formatbuf, p->data.dnum)` (line 394): the visible clamps (lines 357-358, 367-375) bound `%f` output to <= sizeof(work)-1 chars; overflow would require `maxprec` (size_t, line 367) to wrap, i.e., BUFFSIZE <= 310, which is unshown.
`width = -width;` (line 109) overflows when width == LONG_MIN (UB), but width only feeds output-padding loops that skip on negative values; no security-relevant downstream use is shown.
FORMAT_INTPTR `%n` writes (lines 406-415) trust the caller-supplied pointer type; no bad pointer producer exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment alone. Both decode branches derive in-domain destination capacities (base64: size = hts_base64_decoded_length(strlen(data)) at L13-L14; percent: size = strlen(data)+1 at L19-L20), and every visible hazard is guarded (comma NULL at L6, mode 'r' at L10, comma-url >= 7 before &comma[-7] at L12, malloc NULL at L15/L21, hfile_init_fixed NULL at L27). The only plausible overflow (write past the base64 buffer at L16) would require hts_decode_base64 to emit more bytes than hts_base64_decoded_length(strlen(data)) — unshown callee behavior beyond its name-implied contract — so it cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

assumptions: url and mode are valid non-NULL C strings; the fragment neither establishes nor contradicts this, and NULL would be a caller-contract premise rather than a value produced inside the shown code.

By name and use, hts_base64_decoded_length(n) is the maximum byte count a conforming base64 decode of n chars can emit, and hts_decode_base64 writes at most that many bytes and stores the count in *length.
By name and use, percent decoding (%XX -> 1 byte) is length-reducing or equal, so strlen(data)+1 at L19 covers all possible decode output including a NUL terminator.

hfile_init_fixed(sizeof(hFILE_mem), mode, buffer, length, size) receives buf_size=length and buf_alloc=size and takes ownership of buffer on success, as implied by buffer being freed only on the L27 failure path.
malloc(0) for an empty base64 payload is implementation-defined but safe on both outcomes (NULL -> error return; non-NULL -> zero-byte decode).
limitations: Heap-buffer-overflow via hts_decode_base64 (CWE-787) is not confirmable: the buffer capacity at L14 equals hts_base64_decoded_length(strlen(data)), the name-implied decode bound, so an overflow would depend on unshown callee behavior (e.g., word-at-a-time tail writes) that the fragment cannot establish.

The base64 branch allocates no +1 for a NUL terminator (L13-L14); a 1-byte OOB read could only occur if some unshown consumer (hfile_init_fixed/mem_backend) requires NUL-terminated buffer content, which the fragment does not show.

Return values of hts_decode_base64 (L16) and hts_decode_percent (L22) are discarded; if either reports a failure and leaves length unset, L26 would consume a stale value. Their return types and error contracts are not visible, so the CWE-754-style flaw is unconfirmed.

malloc sizes derive from attacker-controlled strlen(data) (L13-L14, L19-L20) with no cap, but the URL is already resident memory and the allocation is one-shot with no visible volume amplification, so CWE-400 is not confirmed.
NULL url or mode would fault at L5/L10, but no statement in the fragment makes NULL reachable from inside the shown code.
Empty base64 data (URL ending ';base64,') yields malloc(0); behavior is implementation-defined but memory-safe on both outcomes.

The base64 marker check at L12 recognizes only the exact 7-byte suffix ';base64' immediately before the comma; other spellings fall into the percent branch and are mis-decoded with no memory-safety impact visible.

verdict.summary: Stack out-of-bounds write in case FORMAT_DOUBLE: width/precision are appended into `char formatbuf[32]` (L330) with `fptr` advanced past up to 4 flag bytes (L348-354) while `left` (L332) is never reduced for them, so an admitted format such as "%#-+ 9223372036854775807.9223372036854775807lf" makes the precision write at L366 (maxlength 12 at `&formatbuf[24]`) NUL-terminate at index 35, then `'l'` at L370, `'f'` at L377 and the final NUL at L379 write indices 35-37 — 4-6 bytes past the 32-byte capacity (CWE-787). All shown guards admit the witness: L358 (`width >= 0`) and L364 (`prec >= 0`) only test sign; no shown statement bounds width/precision magnitude. The width/precision provenance is an internal-helper parameter (format/va_arg driven), so exploitability depends on the unshown call chain.

evidence.reason: Precision-write sink: for format "%#-+ 9223372036854775807.9223372036854775807lf", Pass1-derived p->width/p->precision (L337, L343) have the full long domain (no shown cap). Flags at L348-354 advance fptr to &formatbuf[5] while left stays 31 (L332); the width write at L360 leaves fptr=&formatbuf[24], left=12; this call writes 11 chars plus a NUL at index 24+11=35, four bytes past the declared 32-byte capacity `char formatbuf[32]` at L330 (valid indices 0..31). The admitted-set witnesses are 9223372036854775807, admitted by L358 (width >= 0) and L364 (prec >= 0); a standard msnprintf-family call writes up to maxlength bytes (NUL-terminated) from the given pointer, so the shown pointer+length arguments are out of domain. OOB write -> CWE-787.

After the L366 precision write, fptr points at index 35, already beyond formatbuf's 0..31 capacity (L330); this in-fragment dereference writes the conversion character at index 36, extending the stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Reachable with the same witness admitted by L358 and L364; no sink-side bound check exists between L367 and L377.

Final NUL written through fptr that has advanced to index 37 (with FLAGS_LONG at L369-370 writing 'l' at 35 and L377 writing 'f' at 36) for the same witness; formatbuf[37] is six bytes past the L330 capacity of 32 bytes, an out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787).

assumptions: `char formatbuf[32]` at L330 has capacity 32 bytes (valid indices 0..31) — declared capacity visible in the fragment.
LP64 platform: `long` is 64-bit, so LONG_MAX = 9223372036854775807 (19 decimal digits).

`p->width`/`p->precision` (L337/L343) hold the full parsed literal/parameter value; no statement in the fragment constrains them, so they retain the full long domain. The finding also holds if the width field is only `int` (10-digit cap): with 4 flags the precision write still NUL-terminates at index 35.

`curl_msnprintf` behaves as the standard bounded msnprintf family (NUL-terminating, at most `maxlength` bytes from the supplied pointer); only the first out-of-bounds byte (the NUL at index 35) depends on this, since the writes at L370/L377/L379 are directly in the fragment.
`dprintf_Pass1` (unseen) populates `vto`/`endpos` and sets `p->flags`, `p->type`, `p->width`, `p->precision`; the fragment itself adds no constraint on their values.
limitations: Attacker control of the internal-helper parameter `format` (and of width/precision values derived from it) is not established within the fragment; exploitability depends on the unshown caller chain, so severity/confidence are calibrated accordingly.

`while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';` (L207-208) writes `prec` bytes below `work[0]` for large admitted precisions, and `(sprintf)(work, formatbuf, p->data.dnum)` (L383) can overflow `work` when formatbuf still contains huge width/precision; both objects' capacity is `work[BUFFSIZE]` (L25) whose numeric value is not shown, so the exact boundary/excess is unconfirmable.

`p = &vto[param]` (L99), `vto[p->width]` (L103/L339), `vto[p->precision]` (L119/L345) and `f = *end++` (L407) bounds depend on the unshown `dprintf_Pass1` validation and the unshown `MAX_PARAMETERS` value.

`width = -width` (L109) with width == LONG_MIN is a signed-integer overflow (UB); on wrapping implementations the later `while(--width > 0)` (L144-145) can spin ~2^63 iterations. Demoted because the failure depends on UB wrap semantics.
The missing `left -= len;` after L367 feeds no later use of `left` in the fragment, so it has no demonstrated security impact.
Huge-width output loops (`while(width-- > 0) OUTCHAR(...)`) reflect standard printf semantics and terminate for non-wrapping widths; not reported as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled precinct geometry makes prcno reach assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs) at line 74: prcno is computed at lines 66-72 from x/y that are bounded only by [xstart,xend)/[ystart,yend) (lines 42-45) with no shown relation to numhprcs/numprcs, and no shown check bounds prchind/prcvind. A codestream whose x extent spans more precinct columns than the grid admits (e.g., one vertical precinct, prchind = numhprcs) yields prcno >= numprcs through every earlier guard (lines 50, 54, 62-65), aborting the process. The same out-of-domain index drives the read/write at prclyrnos[pi->prcno] (lines 77-79) if the assert is removed by NDEBUG, but that write is not independently confirmed because the array capacity is not declared in the fragment.

evidence.reason: prcno is derived at lines 66-72 as prcvind * numhprcs + prchind from x,y whose only shown bounds are [xstart,xend)/[ystart,yend) (lines 42-45); no shown statement bounds prchind below numhprcs, prcvind, or prcno below numprcs. Entry-point (codestream-derived) residual range therefore includes prcno >= numprcs: with a single vertical precinct (numprcs == numhprcs) and xend spanning numhprcs+1 precinct columns, a grid-aligned x admitted by line 63 gives prchind == numhprcs and prcno == numprcs, passing guards at lines 50, 54, and 62-65 unchanged. The invariant asserted at line 74 is established nowhere in the fragment, so the fail-assert is attacker-reachable (CWE-617); under NDEBUG the same index reaches the heap read/write at lines 77-79 via prclyrnos[pi->prcno]. The write's array capacity is not declared in the fragment, so the OOB write itself is confined to limitations.

assumptions: numprcs (lines 54, 74) is the precinct count that the asserted invariant treats as the exclusive upper bound of prclyrnos indexing, and numhprcs (line 72) is the precincts-per-row count used by the linear index prcvind*numhprcs + prchind.
Fields of pi/pchg/picomp/pirlvl are populated from the codestream by the caller; within this fragment they are unconstrained except by the checks quoted in the analysis.
limitations: Concrete numeric witness values are not enumerated because the declared types (signedness/width) of jpc_pchg_t/jpc_picomp_t/jpc_pirlvl_t members are outside the fragment; the confirmed witness is the residual admitted range (prchind >= numhprcs with numvprcs == 1).

Heap out-of-bounds write at line 79 (subscript at line 77, read at line 78) is not reported as an independent verdict: the allocation/capacity of prclyrnos is not identifiable from the fragment, the assert's bound may not equal the array capacity (capacity-grounding rule), and the write executes only when NDEBUG removes the assert, which is not shown.

Negative pchg->rlvlnostart/compnostart would allow out-of-bounds reads at lines 47 and 53, but the signedness of those members is not shown, so attacker control of a negative start cannot be demonstrated.

Division-by-zero and undefined-shift candidates (lines 29-32, 43, 45, 60-63) require zero or overflowing exponents/hsamp/vsamp whose magnitudes cannot be derived from the fragment; benign geometry produces positive steps and terminating loops.
Loop non-termination via xstep/ystep <= 0 (lines 42-45) depends on the same unshown member types.

The goto skip resume path (line 21) presumes the caller established prgvolfirst == 1 on the first call; a first call with prgvolfirst == 0 would skip step initialization (caller-contract dependent, not demonstrated).
